His blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, respiratory rate is 11 breaths/minute, and heart rate is 60 beats/minute. Pupils are constricted and bowel sounds are decreased. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medication to administer?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Naloxone: This patient is suffering from opioid intoxication , as indicated by his clinical presentation. Signs of opioid intoxication include depressed mental status, miosis, decreased respiratory rate and tidal volume; decreased bowel sounds, nausea, vomiting, and severe itching . The patient's heart rate can be normal to low. Hypotension may occur as a result of histamine release, but it is not consistently seen. Overdose that involves opioid drugs is a life-threatening situation. Fatal respiratory depression can occur due to direct suppression of respiratory centers in the midbrain and medulla. Naloxone is a strong antagonist of µ-opioid receptors , a medium antagonist of kappa-opioid receptors, and a weak antagonist of delta-opioid receptors. Opioid intoxication is treated with naloxone, adequate hydration, mechanical ventilation. Incorrect Options: Option A- Acamprosate: Acamprosate is an anti-craving drug used for maintenance therapy of alcohol withdrawal. Option B- Bupropion: Bupropion is used for nicotine withdrawal and acts on dopamine and noradrenaline receptors. Option C- Buprenorphine : Buprenorphine is used for detoxification and as part of maintenance therapy for opioid withdrawal. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male with 5-year history of schizophrenia is brought to the ER unconscious by his parents . He is taking trifluoperazine. Examination reveals BP: 175/110, Temperature: 102 Fahrenheit, sweating, confusion, disorientation, and increased muscle tone. Lab results indicate a high white count, and impaired renal function. Which of the following is the best pharmacological intervention in this case?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male with 5-year history of schizophrenia is brought to the ER unconscious by his parents . He is taking trifluoperazine. Examination reveals BP: 175/110, Temperature: 102 Fahrenheit, sweating, confusion, disorientation, and increased muscle tone. Lab results indicate a high white count, and impaired renal function. Which of the following is the best pharmacological intervention in this case?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Bromocriptin: The patient is suffering from neuroleptic malignant syndrome , which is a serious adverse effect of typical antipsychotics mostly seen in young males. It can occur anytime during the course of treatment with antipsychotics. It is characterized by increased temperature, elevated blood pressure, tachycardia, tremors, altered consciousness, muscle rigidity, dystonia, mutism, akinesia, agitation, and sweating. Lab investigations mostly reveal elevated CPK levels, raised WBC, deranged liver and renal functions, and deranged serum electrolytes. Symptoms evolve over 24-72 hours, and untreated syndrome lasts for 10-14 hours. Aggressive supportive care is the first line of treatment. Complications may include electrolyte imbalance, acute renal failure with rhabdomyolysis, dehydration, cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure from chest wall rigidity, seizures from hypothermia or metabolic derangements, cardiomyopathy, DIC, DVT, and hepatic failure. Discontinuation of any neuroleptic drug is essential. In addition to IV fluid maintenance, control of fever and blood pressure are important. Heparin or LMWH are used to prevent DVT. Other pharmacological treatment recommendations are based upon clinical expertise and case studies and there is no clear evidence of efficacy. Pharmacologic agents commonly used in treatment of NMS include dantrolene, bromocriptine, and amantadine. Incorrect Options: Option A- Haloperidol: Haloperidol is a typical antipsychotic and will worsen the condition of patient who is already suffering from neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Option B- Propranolol: Propranolol is a beta blocker and drug of choice in acute akathisia. Option D- Lorazepam: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine with sedative properties and mostly used in neuroleptic-induced akathisia. It is used in NMS to control agitation, but the patient in this case is unconscious, so it is not indicated. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Angiography : Numbness after trauma is a significant finding in any case. The mechanism in this case is significant enough to disrupt ligaments, and complete dislocations of the knee often spontaneously reduce. This patient’s injury is concerning for popliteal artery injury and must be ruled out with angiogram . The collection of blood can also compress the nerves in the area resulting in the numbness seen in the question. Failure to detect a vascular injury could lead to a situation where amputation becomes necessary. Aspiration would likely reveal blood in the joint or fat if a fracture is present but adds little to the diagnosis. Plain films and non-contrast CT fail to evaluate vascular structures. Incorrect Options: Option A- Plain films of knee: Plain films may show an effusion but would not show vasculature. Option B- CT imaging (non-contrast): Non-contrast CT will not show vascular details unless there is calcification of the vessel. questions.stem: Which of the following theories of aging in geriatric medicine suggests that aging is primarily driven by the accumulation of DNA damage and mutations over time?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following theories of aging in geriatric medicine suggests that aging is primarily driven by the accumulation of DNA damage and mutations over time?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Free Radical Theory: This theory posits that aging is mainly a result of the cumulative damage caused by reactive oxygen species (free radicals) on cellular structures, particularly DNA. Over time, this damage can lead to mutations and other cellular changes associated with aging. Incorrect Options: Option B - Wear and Tear Theory: This theory suggests that aging is a result of the body wearing out over time due to repeated use and environmental stress. While this theory has some validity, it does not focus on DNA damage and mutations as the primary drivers of aging. Option C - Programmed Aging Theory: The Programmed Aging Theory proposes that aging is genetically programmed and follows a predetermined pattern. This theory implies that aging is not solely a result of DNA damage and mutations, making it an incorrect choice for this question. Option D - Hormonal Theory: The Hormonal Theory of aging posits that changes in hormone levels play a significant role in the aging process. It emphasizes the role of hormones such as insulin, growth hormone, and sex hormones. While hormonal changes are associated with aging, they are not primarily linked to DNA damage and mutations, making this option incorrect. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Calcium gluconate: This patient experienced cardiac arrest while undergoing magnesium infusion, which is concerning for acute magnesium toxicity . Magnesium sulfate is a medication used for the prevention of seizures. Side effects may commonly include nausea, vomiting, and flushing. Rare but serious side effects include somnolence, loss of patellar reflex, and respiratory depression, resulting ultimately in respiratory arrest/cardiac arrest as seen in this patient. Treatment for magnesium toxicity is calcium gluconate. Incorrect Options: Option A - Potassium chloride: Potassium chloride is given to patients with low potassium. questions.stem: Which of the following is a regulatory protein that promotes cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a regulatory protein that promotes cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Bcl-2 Bcl-2, also known as B-cell lymphoma 2, is an anti-apoptotic regulatory protein that plays a crucial role in promoting cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis. It is a member of the Bcl-2 family of proteins, which regulate the intrinsic or mitochondrial pathway of apoptosis. Bcl-2 is located in the outer mitochondrial membrane and functions to prevent the release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors from the mitochondria, thus blocking the activation of the apoptosis cascade. By inhibiting the pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BAK, Bcl-2 helps to maintain the integrity of the mitochondrial membrane and prevent cell death, promoting cell survival. Incorrect Options: Option A - BAX: BAX is a pro-apoptotic protein belonging to the Bcl-2 family. It promotes apoptosis by forming channels in the mitochondrial membrane, leading to the release of cytochrome c and initiating the apoptosis cascade. BAX acts opposite to Bcl-2 and promotes cell death. Option B - BAK: Like BAX, BAK is also a pro-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 family. It is involved in the permeabilization of the mitochondrial membrane and the release of cytochrome c, triggering apoptosis. BAK works similarly to BAX and promotes cell death. Option D - BAD: BAD is another pro-apoptotic protein belonging to the Bcl-2 family. It acts by binding and inhibiting anti-apoptotic proteins like Bcl-2 and Bcl-XL. Inhibition of these anti-apoptotic proteins can lead to the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins like BAX and BAK, promoting apoptosis. So, BAD is involved in promoting cell death rather than inhibiting it. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following would be considered a contraindication for receiving radiation therapy in the adjuvant setting for seminoma?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following would be considered a contraindication for receiving radiation therapy in the adjuvant setting for seminoma?
questions.solution: Correct Option C-Ulcerative colitis: In the adjuvant setting for seminoma, radiation therapy is often used to prevent the recurrence of cancer after surgical removal of the tumor. However, there are certain medical conditions or contraindications that may affect a patient's eligibility for radiation therapy. In this case, ulcerative colitis would be considered a contraindication for receiving radiation therapy in the adjuvant setting for seminoma. Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that affects the colon and rectum. Radiation therapy can exacerbate gastrointestinal symptoms and potentially worsen the condition in patients with ulcerative colitis. The radiation can further irritate and damage the already inflamed and sensitive gastrointestinal tract, leading to increased discomfort and complications. Therefore, individuals with ulcerative colitis would typically not be candidates for radiation therapy as part of their cancer treatment. Incorrect Options: Option A- Chronic kidney disease: Chronic kidney disease alone is not necessarily a contraindication for radiation therapy in the adjuvant setting for seminoma. However, the radiation oncologist would need to take the patient's kidney function into consideration when planning the treatment, as the kidneys are sensitive to radiation. Adjustments in the radiation dose and treatment planning may be necessary to minimize the risk of kidney damage. Option B- Insulin-dependent diabetes: Insulin-dependent diabetes, also known as type 1 diabetes, is not a direct contraindication for receiving radiation therapy. However, individuals with diabetes may require careful monitoring and management of their blood sugar levels during radiation therapy. Radiation therapy can affect blood sugar levels, and healthcare providers need to work closely with diabetic patients to ensure their blood sugar remains well-controlled during treatment. Option D- Hypertension: Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is not typically a contraindication for radiation therapy. However, healthcare providers should monitor and manage a patient's blood pressure during treatment to minimize any potential complications. Radiation therapy can affect blood vessels, so individuals with hypertension may require close monitoring and adjustments to their blood pressure medications as needed. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Exon 20 insertion: Exon 20 insertion mutation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is NOT sensitive to reversible (erlotinib or gefitinib) or irreversible (neratinib or afatinib) EGFR inhibitors. Thus, patients with newly diagnosed stage IV non-small cell lung cancer who harbour this EGFR mutation should NOT be treated with an EGFR inhibitor as first-line therapy. Instead, they should be treated with chemotherapy or other targeted agents (depending on the status of ALK, ROS1, and PD-L1 expression). Up to 4% of EGFR mutations are an exon 20 insertion, which is generally located at the C-helix of the tyrosine kinase domain. Preclinical studies of this mutation demonstrated resistance to EGFR inhibitors, and a clinical study revealed that 17 of 20 patients with this mutation treated with an EGFR inhibitor had progression as the best response . questions.solution: Correct Option C - Kell antigen: In patients with sickle cell anemia who receive multiple blood transfusions, there is an increased risk of developing alloimmunization, which is the production of antibodies against foreign antigens present on donor red blood cells. This immune response can lead to difficulty finding compatible blood for future transfusions. The Kell antigen system is one of the clinically significant blood group systems, and antibodies against Kell antigens are relatively common. The Kell antigen is present on the surface of red blood cells and can elicit an immune response when a person without the Kell antigen is exposed to it through transfusion. Incorrect Options: Option A - I antigen: The I antigen system is part of the ABO blood group system. Antibodies against the I antigen are not typically associated with alloimmunization in the context of sickle cell anemia. Option B - P antigen: The P antigen is part of the P blood group system. Antibodies against the P antigen are associated with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria and are less commonly seen in the context of sickle cell anemia and blood transfusions. Option D - Rh antigen: The Rh antigen system is part of the Rh blood group system. Antibodies against Rh antigens, particularly RhD, are common and can lead to hemolytic disease of the newborn and transfusion reactions. While Rh antibodies are relevant, the question focuses on antibodies developed due to blood transfusions in the context of sickle cell anemia. The Kell antigen system is a more likely cause of alloimmunization in this scenario. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Inter-strand DNA cross-link repair defect: Fanconi anemia (FA) is characterized by a genetic defect in the pathway responsible for repairing inter-strand DNA cross-links. When these cross-links, which connect the two DNA strands together, are not repaired, it results in genomic instability. The Fanconi anemia protein complex plays a critical role in the recognition and repair of these cross-links. The failure of this repair process can lead to bone marrow failure, which is a hallmark of FA. Incorrect Options: Option B - Intra-strand DNA cross-links repair defect: This choice refers to defects within a single strand of DNA, where certain adjacent nucleotides are linked together. FA is specifically associated with inter-strand, not intra-strand, cross-link repair. Option C - Double-stranded DNA brake repair defect: Double-stranded DNA breaks, where both DNA strands are broken, are indeed dangerous lesions. While the Fanconi anemia pathway interacts with the machinery that repairs double-strand breaks, the primary defect in FA isn't a failure to repair these breaks but rather a failure to repair inter-strand cross-links. Option D - Chromosome break point repair defect: While patients with FA often exhibit increased chromosomal breakage, especially when exposed to cross-linking agents like diepoxybutane or mitomycin-C (used in diagnostic tests for FA), the primary defect isn't in repairing "break points" per se. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Factor 13 deficiency: Factor XIII, also known as fibrin-stabilizing factor, plays a critical role in the final stages of the blood clotting cascade. questions.stem: A 42-year-old gentleman is day 185 from a matched sibling donor transplant for idiopathic aplastic anemia. He states that for the last several weeks he has had progressive dysphagia to food. Patient undergoes endoscopy showing narrowing of the distal esophagus with noted desquamation. What is the ideal mode of management?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old gentleman is day 185 from a matched sibling donor transplant for idiopathic aplastic anemia. He states that for the last several weeks he has had progressive dysphagia to food. Patient undergoes endoscopy showing narrowing of the distal esophagus with noted desquamation. What is the ideal mode of management?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Prednisone 2mg/kg: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) can affect various organ systems, including the gastrointestinal tract. GVHD of the gastrointestinal tract can lead to symptoms such as dysphagia, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Treatment for GVHD typically involves immunosuppressive therapy to control the immune response and reduce inflammation. High-dose corticosteroids, such as prednisone, are often the initial treatment of choice. In this case, the recommended treatment is prednisone at a dose of 2mg/kg, which is a standard approach to manage GVHD. The goal is to suppress the aberrant immune response responsible for the tissue damage. Incorrect Options: Option A - Observation: Given the patient's symptoms and the findings on endoscopy, observation alone is not an appropriate management strategy. Dysphagia and esophageal strictures can significantly impact the patient's quality of life and nutritional status. Prompt intervention is needed. Option B - Endoscopic balloon dilation: While endoscopic balloon dilation can be a valuable procedure for managing benign esophageal strictures, it typically addresses structural narrowing of the esophagus and may not target the underlying cause of the stricture, which in this case may be GVHD. Treating the underlying GVHD with immunosuppressive therapy is essential. Option C - Swallow study: A swallow study (also known as a modified barium swallow or videofluoroscopy) is a diagnostic test used to assess swallowing function. While it can provide valuable information about the mechanics of swallowing, it does not address the underlying cause of dysphagia, which appears to be GVHD in this case. Treatment is needed to manage the GVHD-related inflammation causing the dysphagia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - IgA deficiency: IgA deficiency is one of the immunoglobulin deficiencies frequently seen in patients with cGVHD. Incorrect Options: Option A - IgG deficiency: While IgG deficiency can occur in some cases of cGVHD, it is not as commonly associated with this condition as IgA deficiency. IgG is the most abundant immunoglobulin and plays a vital role in systemic immunity. Option C - IgM deficiency: IgM deficiency is less commonly observed in cGVHD compared to IgA deficiency. IgM is the first immunoglobulin produced during an immune response and is associated with early defense against infections. Option D - IgE deficiency: IgE deficiency is not a common finding in cGVHD. IgE is primarily associated with allergic and hypersensitivity reactions and may not be directly related to cGVHD. @Neet_pg_bot

His arterial blood gas while breathing room air reveals a PaO2 of 23 mmHg and a PaCO2 of 16 mmHg. Assuming a respiratory exchange ratio of 0.8 and ignoring water vapour pressure, what is his alveolar-arterial (A-a) O2 gradient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - 10: The alveolar gas equation is as follows: PAO2 = [FIO2 x (Patm – PH20)] – PCO2/R. When going up in altitude, Patm (atmospheric pressure) drops, while FIO 2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) stays constant at 0.21. Plugging in 0.21 for FIO 2 , 253 for Patm, 0.8 for R (respiratory exchange ratio), and 0 for PH 2 O (water vapor pressure) results in a PAO 2 (alveolar partial pressure of oxygen) of 33. Therefore, the difference between PAO 2 and PaO 2 (arterial partial pressure of oxygen) is 33 – 23 = 10 mmHg. questions.stem: A 29-year-old male presents to your OPD. He is seeking a regular physical examination as well as a consultation regarding dizziness and headaches he experienced the last time he ascended a mountain. These symptoms eventually went away after his team camped in the same location for an extra day. He is otherwise healthy, and his examination is completely unremarkable. The patient has no past medical history of concern. Which of the following is the best recommendation to avoid or prevent these symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old male presents to your OPD. He is seeking a regular physical examination as well as a consultation regarding dizziness and headaches he experienced the last time he ascended a mountain. These symptoms eventually went away after his team camped in the same location for an extra day. He is otherwise healthy, and his examination is completely unremarkable. The patient has no past medical history of concern. Which of the following is the best recommendation to avoid or prevent these symptoms?

options.label: A
options.text: No further climbing due to life-threatening illness risk last time

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Acetazolamide: The most appropriate preventive measure for acute mountain sickness for this patient is acetazolamide. Acute mountain sickness (AMS) generally occurs at >2500 meters; however, it has been reported at lower altitudes. AMS is a syndrome of nonspecific manifestations that can develop within 6-12 hours. Patients experience headaches, dizziness, fatigue, and/or nausea with little to no physical exam findings. The most prominent risk factors for developing altitude illness are a history of altitude illness and the rate of ascent. Why this occurs is still unknown, but MR studies suggest that vasogenic cerebral edema is a component of high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE), which is on a spectrum with AMS. The prevention and treatment of AMS include a gradual ascent allowing acclimation, which is how this patient had a resolution of his symptoms on his prior climb. There is thought to be individual variation, but a graded ascent of at most 400 meters above 3000 meters is recommended. Another measure that is thought to be protective is exposure to high altitudes within 2 months of the intended climb, which may lower rates of AMS by 50%. Hydration is important in preventing dehydration secondary to insensible losses (sweating hyperventilation). In regards to pharmacological prevention of AMS, acetazolamide is the drug of choice. Acetazolamide inhibits renal carbonic anhydrase, causing bicarbonate diuresis with subsequent metabolic acidosis and hyperventilation with a relative risk reduction of 48% vs. placebo. Incorrect Options: Option A - No further climbing due to life-threatening illness risk last time: The patient's symptoms of dizziness and headaches during mountain climbing are likely due to acute mountain sickness (AMS), which is not a life-threatening condition. However, any indication of high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) or high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), which are more severe forms of altitude illness, would require immediate descent due to the potential life-threatening nature of these conditions. Option C - Ginkgo biloba: Ginkgo biloba has not been shown to be effective in the prevention of acute mountain sickness (AMS). The most effective pharmacological prevention for AMS is acetazolamide. Option D - Spironolactone: Spironolactone is not used for the prevention of acute mountain sickness (AMS). Acetazolamide is the drug of choice for pharmacological prevention of AMS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A lacrosse athlete, age 21, visits the doctor for his yearly physical examination. The results of pulmonary function studies indicate a 90% FEV1 and a 3600 mL FVC. To evaluate airway impedance, whole-body plethysmography is used. Which of the following respiratory tree components is most likely to contribute the most to overall lung resistance?
questions.stemHtml: A lacrosse athlete, age 21, visits the doctor for his yearly physical examination. The results of pulmonary function studies indicate a 90% FEV1 and a 3600 mL FVC. To evaluate airway impedance, whole-body plethysmography is used. Which of the following respiratory tree components is most likely to contribute the most to overall lung resistance?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Segmental bronchi: Due to their small overall cross-sectional area, intermediate-sized bronchi, particularly segmental bronchi, are the main causes of airway obstruction. Although there is less airway resistance in a single big airway than in a single small airway, the overall airway resistance is drastically reduced due to the increased cross-sectional area of the numerous parallel pathways. In addition, laminar airflow occurs in tiny passages, further reducing lung resistance. This explains why less than 20% of the overall airway resistance is accounted for by small airways (less than 2 millimetres in diameter). Incorrect Options: Option B - Conducting bronchioles: Despite their big cross-sectional area and high quantity, conducting bronchioles do not make up most of the airway resistance. Option C - Alveolar ducts: The respiratory tree's alveolar ducts have the narrowest width and, consequently, the greatest impedance per unit length. Despite their exceedingly high quantity and huge total cross-sectional area, they are not the main contributors to total airway resistance. Option D - Terminal bronchioles: Despite their tiny diameter, the terminal bronchioles are typically part of the respiratory tree that adds the least to overall airway resistance due to their high number and wide cross-sectional area. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Segmental bronchi:

  • Due to their small overall cross-sectional area, intermediate-sized bronchi, particularly segmental bronchi, are the main causes of airway obstruction. 
  • Although there is less airway resistance in a single big airway than in a single small airway, the overall airway resistance is drastically reduced due to the increased cross-sectional area of the numerous parallel pathways. 
  • In addition, laminar airflow occurs in tiny passages, further reducing lung resistance. 
  • This explains why less than 20% of the overall airway resistance is accounted for by small airways (less than 2 millimetres in diameter).

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Conducting bronchioles:

  • Despite their big cross-sectional area and high quantity, conducting bronchioles do not make up most of the airway resistance.

Option C - Alveolar ducts:

  • The respiratory tree's alveolar ducts have the narrowest width and, consequently, the greatest impedance per unit length. 
  • Despite their exceedingly high quantity and huge total cross-sectional area, they are not the main contributors to total airway resistance.

Option D - Terminal bronchioles:

  • Despite their tiny diameter, the terminal bronchioles are typically part of the respiratory tree that adds the least to overall airway resistance due to their high number and wide cross-sectional area.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old lady visits the emergency room after experiencing significant shortness of breath for the past 12 hours and a worsening of her persistent cough. She suffers from chronic obstructive lung disease and hypertension. According to pulse oximetry, room air has an oxygen concentration of 82%. Subcostal retractions and perioral cyanosis are visible upon examination. The patient is administered Albuterol, injectable methylprednisolone, and 100% oxygen at 10 L/min. Eight hours later, she becomes unresponsive and sleepy. Which of the following describes the somnolence of this patient most accurately?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old lady visits the emergency room after experiencing significant shortness of breath for the past 12 hours and a worsening of her persistent cough. She suffers from chronic obstructive lung disease and hypertension. According to pulse oximetry, room air has an oxygen concentration of 82%. Subcostal retractions and perioral cyanosis are visible upon examination. The patient is administered Albuterol, injectable methylprednisolone, and 100% oxygen at 10 L/min. Eight hours later, she becomes unresponsive and sleepy. Which of the following describes the somnolence of this patient most accurately?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Increased arterial Pco2: The most probable cause of this patient's somnolence is increased arterial pCO2 brought on by increased supplemental oxygen. To prevent oxygen-induced hypercapnia and CO2 narcosis, as seen here, oxygen treatment in patients with persistently compromised oxygenation from COPD should be titrated to a saturation of 88-92%. Alveolar hyperoxia prevents hypoxic lung vasoconstriction, increasing the amount of oxygen delivered to inadequately vented alveoli. (i.e., worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch). The primary cause of acute hypercapnia is believed to be the ensuing increased dead space ventilation. Additionally, increased oxyhemoglobin makes it easier for RBCs to discharge CO2. (Haldane effect). Contrary to expectations, pCO2 only slightly rises due to decreased hypoxia respiratory drive. Incorrect Options: Option B - Decreased cerebral blood flow: Patients with hypocapnia (such as hyperventilating patients) experience decreased brain blood flow due to cerebral vasoconstriction. Neurological impairment, such as vertigo, disorientation, and vision disturbances, can be a symptom of hypocapnia, but somnolence is not a usual symptom. Due to cerebral vasodilation, hypercapnia, which would result in enhanced rather than reduced cerebral blood flow, is more likely to happen in COPD. Option C - Increased pulmonary vasoconstriction: Hypoxemia causes increased pulmonary vasoconstriction (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), which corrects an underlying ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) imbalance and alleviates COPD symptoms. However, this patient's hyperoxemia from excessive oxygen supplementation has exacerbated the V/Q mismatch and clinical appearance by causing vasodilation of capillaries in under-ventilated lungs. Option D - Decreased serum bicarbonate concentration: Reduced blood bicarbonate content is observed in respiratory alkalosis as a compensating shift and in metabolic acidosis (caused, for example, by renal failure, lactic acidosis, or gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonates) (e.g., pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pain, anxiety). But individuals with COPD frequently exhibit lung acidosis due to residual CO2. Therefore, there is likely an increase in serum bicarbonate rather than a decline. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with acute dyspnoea, wheezing, and chest tightness. She reports a history of asthma and has been non-compliant with her medications. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathology of asthma?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with acute dyspnoea, wheezing, and chest tightness. She reports a history of asthma and has been non-compliant with her medications. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathology of asthma?

options.label: C
options.text: Inflammatory cell infiltration in alveolar spaces

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy: Bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy is a key feature of the pathophysiology of asthma. In patients with asthma, the bronchial smooth muscle becomes thicker and larger due to hypertrophy and hyperplasia. This leads to increased airway resistance , decreased airflow , and exacerbation of symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. The smooth muscle hypertrophy in asthma is believed to be due to a combination of chronic inflammation, mechanical stress, and increased responsiveness to growth factors. Inflammation of the airways leads to the release of cytokines and other inflammatory mediators, which stimulate smooth muscle cell proliferation and hypertrophy. Mechanical stress caused by increased airway resistance and stretching of the airways also contributes to smooth muscle hypertrophy. Additionally, asthmatic smooth muscle cells have been shown to be more responsive to growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), which further stimulate hypertrophy and hyperplasia. Incorrect Options: Option B - Alveolar wall thickening: Alveolar wall thickening is a hallmark feature of interstitial lung diseases, such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or sarcoidosis, but not asthma. The thickening of alveolar walls in these conditions can impair gas exchange and lead to progressive lung dysfunction. Option C - Inflammatory cell infiltration in alveolar spaces: Inflammatory cell infiltration in alveolar spaces is not a feature of asthma. While inflammation is a key component of asthma pathophysiology, it occurs primarily in the airway walls and is not typically seen in the alveoli. Option D - Fibrosis of alveolar septa: Fibrosis of alveolar septa is a characteristic finding in conditions such as pulmonary fibrosis, but it is not seen in asthma. Pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive and irreversible lung disease that results in scarring and stiffening of the lung tissue, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory failure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with recurring episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms are only triggered in certain situations, which the patient can’t point out. He also reports coughing and difficulty breathing during exercise. His medical history is significant for eczema. On physical examination, the patient has diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old male presents with recurring episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms are only triggered in certain situations, which the patient can’t point out. He also reports coughing and difficulty breathing during exercise. His medical history is significant for eczema. On physical examination, the patient has diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Allergic asthma: Allergic asthma is the most common form of asthma, accounting for around 50-60% of all asthma cases. It is an immunoglobulin E (Ig E)-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to various allergens, including house dust mites, pollen, animal dander, and moulds. In allergic asthma, allergens are inhaled and processed by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in the airways. These APCs then present allergen peptides to T-helper 2 (Th2) cells, which produce interleukins, such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 . These interleukins activate eosinophils, which release inflammatory mediators such as leukotrienes and prostaglandins, causing bronchial smooth muscle contraction, airway oedema, and mucus production. In addition, Ig E antibodies produced by B cells in response to the allergens bind to mast cells and basophils, triggering the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators. Symptoms of allergic asthma include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, which occur in response to exposure to allergens. Incorrect Options: Option B - Occupational asthma: Occupational asthma is caused by exposure to irritants or allergens in the workplace. It is estimated to account for approximately 5-15% of adult asthma cases. While the patient's symptoms could potentially be caused by occupational asthma, the fact that she has a history of allergies makes allergic asthma a more likely diagnosis. Option C - Exercise-induced asthma: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA) is a type of asthma that is triggered by physical exertion. It is estimated to affect approximately 90% of individuals with asthma. However, in this scenario, the patient's symptoms are not necessarily related to physical exertion, so EIA is less likely to be the cause of her symptoms. Option D - Non-allergic asthma: Non-allergic asthma, also known as intrinsic asthma , is asthma that is not caused by an allergic response. It is estimated to account for approximately 30-40% of adult asthma cases. However, the patient's history of allergies makes allergic asthma a more likely diagnosis than non-allergic asthma. @Neet_pg_bot

On examination, a silent chest is appreciated, and the patient is breathing by supporting his shoulders. A clinical diagnosis of COPD is made. Which of the following pathophysiological finding is most important in this patient?

On examination, a silent chest is appreciated, and the patient is breathing by supporting his shoulders. A clinical diagnosis of COPD is made. Which of the following pathophysiological finding is most important in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased diffusion lung capacity of carbon monoxide

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Increased elastase activity Nicotine and smoking cause the inactivation of protease inhibitors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin, which cause increased activity of elastase resulting in parenchymal and elastic tissue loss. It results in airspaces enlargement, decreased elastic recoil, increased lung compliance and expiratory airway collapse, trapping of air and hyperinflation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increased diffusion lung capacity of carbon monoxide Air trapping causes decreased ventilation resulting in increased dead space and decreased diffusion lung capacity of carbon monoxide (DLCO), and increased ventilation-perfusion mismatch V/Q resulting in hypercapnia and hypoxemia. Option B - Increased elastic recoil In COPD, elastic recoil is decreased, which causes reduced tethering of smaller air passages resulting in expiratory collapse and obstruction, causing air trapping and hypoventilation. Option C - Decreased compliance Air space enlargement causes increased compliance of the lungs, and decreased elastic recoil results in air trapping and hypoventilation. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Nicotine and smoking cause the inactivation of protease inhibitors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin, which cause increased activity of elastase resulting in parenchymal and elastic tissue loss. 
  • It results in airspaces enlargement, decreased elastic recoil, increased lung compliance and expiratory airway collapse, trapping of air and hyperinflation. 

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Increased diffusion lung capacity of carbon monoxide 

  • Air trapping causes decreased ventilation resulting in increased dead space and decreased diffusion lung capacity of carbon monoxide (DLCO), and increased ventilation-perfusion mismatch V/Q resulting in hypercapnia and hypoxemia. 

Option B - Increased elastic recoil 

  • In COPD, elastic recoil is decreased, which causes reduced tethering of smaller air passages resulting in expiratory collapse and obstruction, causing air trapping and hypoventilation. 

Option C - Decreased compliance

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an indication for referring pneumonia patients to the intensive therapy unit (ITU)?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is not an indication for referring pneumonia patients to the intensive therapy unit (ITU)?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - CURB-65 score of 2: The most important aspects of pneumonia management are oxygenation, fluid balance, and antibiotic therapy. Nutritional support may be needed in severe or prolonged cases. Oxygen is given to patients with tachypnoea, hypoxaemia, hypotension, or acidosis. Oxygenation aims to maintain PaO2 at or above 8kPa (60mmHg) or SaO2 at or above 92%. Highly-concentrated and humidified oxygen is used in patients with hypercapnia associated with COPD. Continous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is required for hypoxic patients. These patients are to be managed in a high-dependency or intensive care environment. Indications for referral to the intensive therapy unit (ITU) include the following: CURB-65 score of 4-5 Persistent hypoxia despite the high concentration of oxygen Progressive hypercapnia Severe acidosis Circulatory shock Reduced conscious level Incorrect Options: Option B - Reduced conscious level: A reduced consciousness level is an indication of referral to ITU. Option C - Circulatory shock: Circulatory shock is an indication for referral to ITU. Option D - Progressive hypercapnia: Progressive hypercapnia is an indication for referral to ITU. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a pneumonic complication most likely associated with Staphylococcus aureus only?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Ectopic abscess formation: Patients with pneumonia respond promptly to antibiotics. Fever may persist for several days, and the chest x-ray may take weeks or months to become normal. Delayed recovery may occur due to a complication, incorrect diagnosis, proximal bronchial obstruction, or recurrent aspiration. The complications of pneumonia include: Parapneumonic effusion Empyema Retention of sputum causing a lobar collapse Deep vein thrombosis Pulmonary embolism Pneumothorax Suppurative pneumonia Lung abscess Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) Renal failure Multi-organ failure Ectopic abscess formation Hepatitis Pericarditis Myocarditis Meningoencephalitis Pyrexia due to hypersensitivity Amongst the complications, pneumothorax and ectopic abscess formation are seen particularly with Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia. Incorrect Options: Option A - Parapneumonic effusion: Parapneumonic effusion is a common complication of pneumonia. It is the fluid collection in the pleural space adjacent to pneumonia. It can be seen with pneumonia caused by other organisms and is not specific to Staphylococcus aureus only. Option B - Empyema: Empyema is the collection of pus in the pleural space. It most commonly occurs with bacterial cases of pneumonia and tuberculosis. It is not only caused by Staphylococcal infection but can also be seen with pneumonia caused by other organisms. Option C - Myocarditis: Myocarditis may occur as a complication of pneumonia. It is not specific to Staphylococcal pneumonia and can also occur with pneumonia caused by other organisms. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Aspergillus fumigatus: The patient presents with the clinical features of pneumonia in an immunocompromised individual. The symptoms are less specific in more profound immunosuppressed patients. Investigations usually involve induced sputum for obtaining microbiological samples and imaging. HRCT is the main imaging modality that helps in differentiating the causative agent. A ‘halo sign’ is representative of Aspergillus fumigatus. Incorrect Options: Option B - Pneumocystis jiroveci: Pneumocystis jiroveci may show bilateral opacification and pleural effusions. Option D - Mycobacterium tuberculosis: HRCT findings of Mycobacterium tuberculosis are focal unilateral airspace opacifications and cavitations. A ‘halo sign’ is not seen with a tuberculous infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Alveolar capillary membrane damage: The described clinical scenario is consistent with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), characterized by acute onset dyspnea, severe hypoxemia, and bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging. The primary pathophysiological mechanism in ARDS involves damage to the alveolar capillary membrane. This damage leads to increased permeability, allowing protein-rich fluid to leak into the alveoli, impairing gas exchange. Incorrect Options: Option A- Increased pulmonary compliance: ARDS is associated with decreased pulmonary compliance due to the loss of lung tissue elasticity and surfactant dysfunction. This results in increased stiffness of the lungs, contributing to difficulty in ventilation. Option B- Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance: ARDS is associated with increased pulmonary vascular resistance due to vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling. Pulmonary hypertension is a common feature in the later stages of ARDS. Option D- Enhanced surfactant production: ARDS is characterized by a deficiency of surfactant, leading to increased surface tension and alveolar collapse. Enhanced surfactant production is not a primary pathophysiological mechanism in ARDS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of emergency appendectomy during a trip to his native home in a rural area presents to the emergency department with a high fever, confusion, and a surgical wound in the right lower quadrant with purulent discharge. His vital signs reveal a high temperature, rapid pulse, and low blood pressure. Laboratory studies show an elevated lactate level. His serum sodium and potassium concentrations are within normal limits. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.21 PCO2 36 mm Hg HCO3- 14 mEq/L O2 saturation 87% Which of the following is the likely explanation for these laboratory changes?
questions.stemHtml:
A 47-year-old man with a history of emergency appendectomy during a trip to his native home in a rural area presents to the emergency department with a high fever, confusion, and a surgical wound in the right lower quadrant with purulent discharge. His vital signs reveal a high temperature, rapid pulse, and low blood pressure. Laboratory studies show an elevated lactate level. His serum sodium and potassium concentrations are within normal limits.
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows:
			pH
			7.21
			PCO2
			36 mm Hg
			HCO3-
			14 mEq/L
			O2 saturation
			87%
Which of the following is the likely explanation for these laboratory changes?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Respiratory fatigue This patient has clinical features of septic shock, such as fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and warm and dry skin due to his appendectomy surgical site infection . His metabolic acidosis is likely due to the accumulation of lactic acid from septic shock. Assess for appropriate compensation using the Winter formula: expected pCO2 = (1.5 x HCO3-) + 8 (± 2). Per the Winter formula, a pCO2 of 27–31 mm Hg would reflect an appropriate respiratory compensation for this patient's metabolic acidosis. Instead, this patient's pCO2 is 36 mm Hg, indicating respiratory and metabolic acidosis. Respiratory acidosis is caused by hypoventilation (e.g., from respiratory fatigue in critically ill patients), which leads to CO2 retention. Incorrect options: Option A: Hyperventilation This statement is incorrect, as hyperventilation results in respiratory alkalosis , which manifests with a lower-than-expected pCO2 . questions.solution: Correct Option C: Urine chloride This patient is most likely suffering from primary metabolic alkalosis. This patient's arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.58, PCO2 of 43 mmHg, and HCO3- of 32 mEq/L, consistent with a primary metabolic alkalosis. Measurement of urine chloride concentration is useful to determine the etiology of metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic alkalosis associated with a normal urinary chloride concentration (< 25 mmol/L) is called a chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis because it corrects with the administration of fluid with NaCl. It is often secondary to volume loss through vomiting or diuretic use. Metabolic alkalosis associated with an elevated urinary chloride concentration (> 40 mmol/L) is called a chloride-resistant metabolic alkalosis because it does not correct with the administration of fluid with NaCl. It is often secondary to conditions such as mineralocorticoid excess and is associated with increased extracellular volume and hypertension. Incorrect options: Option A: Urine albumin to creatinine ratio This statement is incorrect as the urine albumin: creatinine ratio identifies glomerular damage and screens for an increased risk of developing kidney disease. Diseases that damage the glomerulus (e.g., diabetes and hypertension) cause excess excretion of albumin, raising the albumin: creatinine ratio. It does not help identify the cause or guide the management of metabolic alkalosis. Option B: Serum osmolal gap This statement is incorrect as measuring the serum osmolal gap is useful in determining the etiology of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis , especially when toxic alcohol ingestion (ethanol, methanol, or ethylene glycol) is being considered. It does not help determine the cause or guide the management of metabolic alkalosis. Option D: Urine anion gap This statement is incorrect because the urine anion gap is used to proxy for NH4+ excretion in the urine, which measures renal acidification . It can be used to determine whether a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis is caused by insufficient renal acidification of urine. questions.solution: Correct Option A: pH and PaCo2 One of the most common methods is to measure the pH and changes in serum bicarbonate levels or partial pressure of carbon dioxide. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is used to calculate acid-base status using three variables: pH, acid, and conjugate base: pH= pK + log {(conjugate base)/(acid)} In the case of the carbon dioxide bicarbonate buffer pair, where CO2 is acid and HCO3 is the conjugate base, the equation is as follows: pH = 6.1 + log (HCO3-)/(0.03 x PaCO2). If the other two variables are given, this equation can be used to calculate the third variable. If the pH and PaCO2 are known, the bicarbonate can be calculated using these three variables. Thus, pH and PaCo2 are the best laboratory investigations to determine the acid-base status of patients. questions.solution: Correct Option C: High anion gap metabolic acidosis High anion gap metabolic acidosis is a medical condition characterized by a high level of acid in the blood, which is typically caused by an increase in the concentration of anions (negatively charged ions) in the blood. This condition is diagnosed when the anion gap, which is the difference between the concentration of positively charged ions (cations) and negatively charged ions (anions) in the blood, is higher than normal. Some of the common causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis include ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, and ingestion of certain toxins, such as methanol or ethylene glycol. The symptoms of this condition may include fatigue, confusion, rapid breathing, and a rapid heartbeat. In severe cases, it can lead to shock, coma, and even death. Treatment of high anion gap metabolic acidosis depends on the underlying cause. For example, if the condition is caused by ketoacidosis, treatment may involve insulin therapy and administration of intravenous fluids to correct the acid-base balance. In some cases, dialysis may be necessary to remove toxins from the blood. Incorrect options: Option A: Respiratory alkalosis Respiratory alkalosis is characterized by an increase in blood pH and a decrease in PaCO2. The patient in this case has a low pH and a normal or slightly decreased PaCO2, indicating that respiratory alkalosis is not the correct diagnosis. Option B: Metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap Metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap is characterized by a decrease in blood pH and a normal anion gap. The anion gap in this case is elevated, suggesting high anion gap metabolic acidosis, which is a distinct type of metabolic acidosis. Option D: Metabolic alkalosis Metabolic alkalosis is characterized by an increase in blood pH and an increase in HCO3-. The patient in this case has a low pH and a decreased HCO3-, indicating that metabolic alkalosis is not the correct diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C: Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation This patient is having microcytic anemia. Despite normal arterial oxygen saturation and partial pressure , anemia lowers arterial oxygen content. Minute ventilation (i.e., respiratory rate and tidal volume ) increases to compensate for the decreased oxygen content, lowering pCO2. pH <7.4 and low pCO2 are associated with primary respiratory alkalosis. This is caused by excessive breathing. Any acid-base (AB) problem, such as acidosis or alkalosis, results in physiological compensation , first through pH buffers in the serum , then through the removal of extra serum acids and bases (such as CO2, H+, and HCO3). questions.solution: Correct Option A - High pH, decreased renal H+ secretion, decreased renal HCO3- reabsorption: Acute high-altitude illness (AHAI) represents a set of pathological symptoms experienced by an unacclimatized individual upon facing hypoxia at high altitudes. AHAI includes acute mountain sickness (AMS), high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), and high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE). High altitude changes result in a reduced partial pressure of oxygen in the blood and an increased partial pressure of carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide-sensitive medullary chemoreceptors increase the rate and depth of breathing for the quick elimination of CO2 from the body, lowering its partial pressure. This leads to the development of respiratory alkalosis, with an increased arterial pH. To compensate, the renal reabsorption of bicarbonates is decreased. Erythropoietin production rises, leading to increased red blood cell production, which improves the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. Hematocrit is also increased by hypoxia-mediated diuresis. Metabolism causes increased carbon dioxide production and hydrogen ion concentration, along with elevated levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. These factors improve oxygen release in the tissues and cause a rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents with complaints of muscle weakness and fatigue. Laboratory results show a potassium level of 2.9 mEq/L (normal range 3.5-5.0 mEq/L). Which of the following drugs is most likely to cause hypokalemia?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female presents with complaints of muscle weakness and fatigue. Laboratory results show a potassium level of 2.9 mEq/L (normal range 3.5-5.0 mEq/L). Which of the following drugs is most likely to cause hypokalemia?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Furosemide Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the reabsorption of sodium , potassium, and chloride by Inhibiting cotransport system (Na + /K + /2Cl − ) of thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle in the kidney, resulting in increased urinary excretion of these electrolytes. Hypokalemia is a common adverse effect of loop diuretics due to their potassium-wasting effect. Incorrect options: Option B: Spironolactone Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks the action of aldosterone, resulting in decreased urinary excretion of potassium and increased retention of sodium. Spironolactone is not likely to cause hypokalemia; in fact, it is often used to treat hypokalemia caused by other diuretics. Option C: Lisinopril Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor that blocks the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, resulting in decreased vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion. Aldosterone directly increases potassium excretion. Thus, low aldosterone by ACE inhibitors cause potassium retention leading to hyperkalemia. Lisinopril is not likely to cause hypokalemia. Option D: Amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker that blocks the entry of calcium into vascular smooth muscle cells, resulting in vasodilation and decreased blood pressure. Gingival hyperplasia, peripheral edema, flushing, and dizziness are adverse effects of amlodipine. Amlodipine is not likely to cause hypokalemia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with a headache, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness after climbing to an altitude of 12,000 feet. Physical examination reveals an unsteady gait, and the patient is diagnosed with mountain sickness. Which of the following diuretics is most useful in the management of mountain sickness?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male presents with a headache, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness after climbing to an altitude of 12,000 feet. Physical examination reveals an unsteady gait, and the patient is diagnosed with mountain sickness. Which of the following diuretics is most useful in the management of mountain sickness?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Acetazolamide Acetazolamide is a diuretic that primarily acts in the proximal tubules of the kidney to inhibit the enzyme carbonic anhydrase . Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the reversible reaction between water and carbon dioxide to form bicarbonate and a hydrogen ion . Inhibition of this enzyme by acetazolamide leads to decreased bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubules , which in turn leads to increased excretion of bicarbonate and a reduction in the reabsorption of sodium and water . When individuals ascend to high altitudes, there is a decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere, which can lead to hypoxia (low oxygen levels) and an increase in carbon dioxide retention . As a result, the body attempts to compensate for this by increasing respiratory rate, heart rate and by increasing bicarbonate reabsorption in the kidneys. Acetazolamide , by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase, can counteract this compensation mechanism by causing an increase in the excretion of bicarbonate, leading to metabolic acidosis . This metabolic acidosis stimulates the respiratory centre in the brain to increase ventilation , which helps to alleviate the symptoms of mountain sickness. In addition, acetazolamide can also cause an increase in urine output , which can help to reduce fluid retention and oedema that can occur at high altitudes . Therefore, acetazolamide is the diuretic of choice in the management of mountain sickness. Incorrect options: Option B: Furosemide Furosemide is a loop diuretic that works in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle in the kidney to inhibit sodium and chloride reabsorption . While furosemide can be an effective treatment for conditions such as oedema and hypertension, it is not typically used in the management of mountain sickness. One reason is that furosemide does not address the underlying cause of mountain sickness , which is a decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen at high altitudes. In contrast, acetazolamide alleviates mountain sickness symptoms by increasing respiratory drive and reducing fluid retention , which helps compensate for the low oxygen levels at high altitudes. Additionally, using furosemide to manage mountain sickness may be counterproductive, as it can lead to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances . This can exacerbate nausea, headache and fatigue associated with mountain sickness. Option C: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic that acts on the distal tubules of the nephron to block the activity of the Na+/Cl- symporter , which normally allows these ions to be reabsorbed into the bloodstream. As a result, sodium and chloride ions are excreted in the urine, leading to increased water excretion. One of the potential side effects of hydrochlorothiazide is metabolic alkalosis , which can occur due to the loss of hydrogen ions in the urine. This can lead to an increase in blood pH and a decrease in bicarbonate ion concentration . Therefore, hydrochlorothiazide would not be effective for the management of mountain sickness as it could potentiate the metabolic alkalosis already present . Instead, treatment for mountain sickness typically involves oxygen therapy, descent to lower altitudes, and the use of medications such as acetazolamide, which can help alleviate symptoms by increasing respiratory drive and reducing the risk of cerebral oedema. Option D: Spironolactone Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic which acts on the late distal tubule and cortical collecting ducts and prevents the aldosterone-mediated exchange of sodium and potassium ions, leading to increased excretion of sodium and decreased excretion of potassium ions. Spironolactone does not affect acid-base balance directly , and hence, it’s not typically used for the management of mountain sickness. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient's medical history reveals that he has not yet experienced any lymphadenopathy. Physical examination shows hypoplasia of lymphoid tissue. Laboratory tests reveal absent or reduced B cells, normal T cell count, and reduced immunoglobulin classes. Genetic analysis confirms a mutation in the BTK gene. questions.solution: Correct Option B - X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA): XLA, also known as Bruton's agammaglobulinemia, is a primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by a mutation in the BTK (Bruton's tyrosine kinase) gene. This mutation results in the failure of B cell maturation and subsequent absence or reduction in immunoglobulins (antibodies), particularly IgM and IgG. Patients with XLA have a characteristic clinical presentation with recurrent pyogenic infections, including pneumonia and otitis media, due to the absence of functional B cells and the resulting inability to produce effective antibody responses. Hypoplasia of lymphoid tissue is also a common finding due to the absence of mature B cells. Incorrect Options: Option A - Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID): CVID is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by decreased levels of immunoglobulins (antibodies) in the blood and a variable age of onset. It usually presents in adolescence or adulthood. While recurrent infections are a feature of CVID, it typically involves both B and T cell defects, and hypoplasia of lymphoid tissue is not a common finding. Option C - Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): SCID is a severe primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by a profound deficiency in both B and T cell function. It usually presents early in life and is associated with severe and recurrent infections. SCID is not likely in this case, as the patient's T cell count is reported as normal, whereas in SCID, both B and T cells are severely affected. Option D - DiGeorge Syndrome: DiGeorge syndrome, also known as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, is a genetic disorder that results from a deletion on chromosome 22. It is characterized by a range of symptoms, including congenital heart defects, hypoparathyroidism, and thymic hypoplasia, leading to T cell deficiency. While T cell deficiency can lead to immunodeficiency, the absence of B cell dysfunction and the reduced immunoglobulin classes seen in this patient are not typical of DiGeorge syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Ventricular premature beats: The broad and bizarre QRS complexes with no preceding P waves between normal sinus beats seen on the ECG are characteristic of VPBs. The irregular pulse and occasionally missed beats are also consistent with VPBs. Ventricular premature beats (VPBs) are ectopic beats that originate from the ventricles rather than the normal pacemaker of the heart, the sinoatrial node. VPBs are commonly found in healthy people, and their prevalence increases with age. VPBs can be asymptomatic or cause palpitations, chest discomfort, and irregular heartbeats. Treatment may not be necessary unless highly symptomatic, but β-blockers or catheter ablation can be used for symptomatic control. Incorrect Options: Option B- Atrial fibrillation: Atrial fibrillation is an irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P waves and narrow QRS complexes. In this scenario, the ECG shows broad and bizarre QRS complexes with no preceding P waves in between normal sinus beats, which is not consistent with atrial fibrillation. questions.solution: Correct Option D- Myocardial biopsy: The most accurate way to diagnose myocarditis is with a myocardial biopsy, which makes it possible to see the inflammatory cells in the heart muscle up close. Incorrect Options: Option A- Cardiac catheterisation: It is uncommon to utilize a test like cardiac catheterisation to identify myocarditis. During this invasive operation, a catheter is inserted into the heart to assess pressure and collect blood samples from the heart chambers. It is not a test specifically for myocarditis, but it can offer important information about how the heart works. Option B- Echocardiography: A non-invasive imaging procedure called echocardiography uses sound waves to produce images of the heart. It can reveal details about the size and operation of the heart as well as whether fluid is present around the organ. Although it can be useful in examining patients who have myocarditis suspicions, it is insufficient to confirm the diagnosis. Option D- Cardiac MRI: Cardiac MRI is a non-invasive imaging procedure that makes precise images of the heart using magnetic fields. It can provide details about the shape, size, and composition of the heart and whether there is any inflammation or scarring. The diagnosis cannot be confirmed with the same accuracy without a myocardial biopsy, although it can be highly helpful in examining patients with suspected myocarditis. @Neet_pg_bot

Option D- NYHA functional class: NYHA functional class is a useful tool for describing the severity of heart failure symptoms, but it has limited predictive value for mortality. questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the hospital because of complaints of fatigue and palpitations. Examination reveals a cyanotic girl and a holo-systolic murmur can be heard over the anterior chest. Echocardiography reveals displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets in the right ventricle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the hospital because of complaints of fatigue and palpitations. Examination reveals a cyanotic girl and a holo-systolic murmur can be heard over the anterior chest. Echocardiography reveals displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets in the right ventricle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Ebstein anomaly: Ebstein anomaly is highly associated with lithium exposure in-utero. In this abnormality the tricuspid valve is abnormally displaced downwards into the right ventricle. All leaflets of the valve apart from the anterior cusp of the valve are adherent to the right ventricular wall. Abnormal tricuspid valve divides the right atrium into two parts: an atrialized portion that is thin-walled and a smaller normal ventricular myocardium-containing portion. Tricuspid valve regurgitation results in the enlargement of the right atrium. A holo-systolic murmur can be heard over most of the left anterior chest. Multiple clicks at the left lower sternal border along with gallop rhythm is also common. In severe cases a combination of tricuspid regurgitation, small poorly functioning ventricles, and obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract by a large tricuspid valve leaflet decreases the effective output of the right heart. Symptoms are mild and may present late in many cases as fatigue and palpitations initially due to cardiac dysrhythmias. Right bundle branch block and broad P-waves that may be normal or tall are ECG findings. Incorrect Options: Option A- Tricuspid atresia: No passage of blood from the right atrium to the right ventricle occurs in this condition and blood enters the left atrium through an atrial septal defect or foramen ovale. Blood from the left ventricle through the aorta enters the systemic circulation and it also mostly flows through VSD to the right ventricle if the great vessels are normally related. If it is associated with transposition of the great vessels, blood from the left ventricle enters the pulmonary artery and for blood to reach the systemic circulation it has to traverse through VSD from the left to right ventricle. Option C- Total anomalous pulmonary venous return: In this condition there is no direct connection between the left atrium and the pulmonary veins and they may drain directly into the right atrium, superior vena cava by a vertical vein, or by a descending vein into the inferior vena cava below the diaphragm. At the level of the right atrium, there is a mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Right ventricular hypertrophy is a common ECG finding. Surgery should be performed for the correction of the abnormality. Option D- Truncus arteriosus: In this condition, the aorticopulmonary septum fails to develop and as a result truncus arteriosus fails to divide into the aorta and pulmonary trunk, and a single arterial trunk supplies pulmonary and systemic circulations. Initial findings in the neonatal period are cyanosis and a murmur over the next few months torrential pulmonary blood flow develops, and heart failure becomes prominent. The second heart sound is single and loud. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman visits the doctor because she has been uncontrollably urinating for the past four months and exacerbated on laughing. She hasn't experienced anxiety or dysuria. She gave birth to all four of her children vaginally. She doesn't take any medicines and is otherwise healthy. Which of the following Nerve is most likely responsible for efferent innervation of the muscles impacted by this patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman visits the doctor because she has been uncontrollably urinating for the past four months and exacerbated on laughing. She hasn't experienced anxiety or dysuria. She gave birth to all four of her children vaginally. She doesn't take any medicines and is otherwise healthy. Which of the following Nerve is most likely responsible for efferent innervation of the muscles impacted by this patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: S2-S4 nerve roots Stress incontinence is the outlet incompetence due to urethral hypermobility: loss of pelvic floor musculature and/or connective tissue support leads to a weak pelvic floor which causes inability of the urethra to completely close. Risk factors Multipara Pregnancy and vaginal deliveries High-impact activity (e.g., jumping, running, hopping) Menopause Obesity Smoking Chronic cough (e.g., COPD) Prostate or pelvic surgery Levator ani and the external urethral sphincter are innervated by somatic neurons that emerge from the S2-S4 spinal cord roots. The pudendal nerve innervates the external urethral sphincter, which emerges from the S2-S4 spinal cord origins and contributes to continence. Stress incontinence is due to compromised pelvic floor support, which can be caused by direct trauma to the levator ani muscle or to nerve roots or by persistently elevated intra-abdominal pressure (for instance, from a chronic cough or obesity). Such direct trauma is more likely to affect multiparous women because complications during birth are more likely to result in it. Rarely can it be caused by intrinsic sphincter abnormalities due to postoperative scarring. Incorrect options: Option B: Obturator nerve The obturator nerve (from L2-L4 nerve roots) innervates the medial leg with sensory information and motor innervation to the obturator externus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, gracilis, and adductor magnus muscles. Hip adduction involves these muscles. Medial thigh sensations and hip adduction are lost when the obturator nerve is injured. It has no impact on how stress leakage manifests. Option C: Superior hypogastric plexus The ovary and ureteric plexus receive sympathetic innervation from the superior hypogastric plexus, which then travels to the ovaries and ureter. Stress incontinence is not a result of this nerve dysfunction because it does not innervate the pelvic floor muscles or the bladder neck. Option D: Superior gluteal nerve The gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fascia lata muscles are all innervated by the superior gluteal nerve (from L4-S1 nerve roots). These muscles help stabilize the hip and Aid in internal rotation and abduction of the hip joint. Trendelenburg gait is the consequence of superior gluteal nerve injury. It has no impact on how stress incontinence manifests. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is admitted to the hospital after he hasn't urinated in 12 hours and has lower back pain. History is positive for Hodgkin lymphoma in the past. An inspection of the body reveals inguinal lymphadenopathy. No suprapubic swelling or tenderness is present. When compared to one week earlier, serum creatinine is higher. An abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scan reveals bilateral hydronephrosis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, and a collapsed bladder. Which of the following represents the ideal course of action for treatment?
questions.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man is admitted to the hospital after he hasn't urinated in 12 hours and has lower back pain. History is positive for Hodgkin lymphoma in the past. An inspection of the body reveals inguinal lymphadenopathy. No suprapubic swelling or tenderness is present. When compared to one week earlier, serum creatinine is higher. An abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scan reveals bilateral hydronephrosis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, and a collapsed bladder. Which of the following represents the ideal course of action for treatment?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Perform a ureteral stenting A ureteral stent is a tiny, hollow tube placed inside the ureter to allow urine from the renal pelvis to drain into the bladder. The most frequent method is transurethral placement guided by cystoscopy, though an antegrade approach using a renal pelvis puncture is also possible. A double-J implant is typically used. The initial treatment for simple upper Urinary Tract Obstruction (UTO) is ureteral stenting. Upper UTO is most likely the result of retroperitoneal fibrosis brought on by Hodgkin lymphoma in this case. Traumatic injury, instrumentation, cancer, infection, and congenital obstruction are some additional frequent reasons. Once the acute obstruction has been removed, further analysis and treatment of the underlying reason are necessary. Incorrect options: Option B: Place a urethral catheter A urethral catheter can avoid a lower urinary system obstruction (e.g., due to benign prostatic hyperplasia, urethral mass, and urethral stricture). A urethral catheter in this patient would not clear a blockage at the level of the ureters because of their empty bladder. Option C: Initiate oxybutynin therapy A muscarinic blocker frequently used to treat bladder spasms is oxybutynin. Anuria and acute renal injury in this patient point to UTO rather than a spastic bladder. Furthermore, oxybutynin is contraindicated in this patient because it can induce urinary obstruction. Option D: Place a suprapubic catheter Complex lower UTO may be treated with suprapubic catheterization. Above the pubic symphysis, a catheter is introduced through the abdominal wall and into the bladder. This patient's obstruction is proximal to the bladder, as observed by an absence of suprapubic fullness and a collapsed bladder on the CT scan; bladder drainage would not resolve the obstruction. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A: Levator ani The levator ani and other minor muscles (like the coccygeus muscle), connective tissue, and other structures comprise most of the pelvic floor. Iliococcygeus, pubococcygeus, and puborectalis muscles clench all simultaneously and make up its three components. Along with the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles in males, these muscles are strengthened by pelvic floor contraction during Kegel exercises. The pubococcygeus should be strengthened as a first-line therapy for urinary incontinence because it enhances urinary retention in both sexes. Men who experience early ejaculation may also benefit from strengthening these muscles. Incorrect Options: Option B: Sphincter urethrae One of the three components of the feminine external urethral sphincter is the urethral sphincter. Together, these voluntary muscles prevent urine from being released. The urethral sphincter is not a focus of kegel exercises. Option C: Deep, transverse perineal muscles The deep, transverse muscles of the perineum are a component of the pelvic floor. The perineal body, a core tendinous structure necessary for the stability of the pelvic floor, is stabilized by these muscles. Kegel exercises do not target the deep, transverse perineal muscles. questions.solution: Correct Option B- Rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI: This patient's diagnosis is consistent with the rhabdomyolysis-induced acute kidney injury, which produced the symptoms of nausea, confusion, vomiting, and an altered level of consciousness. The fluid can enter the damaged tissues and can result in hypotension and shock. Some other complications can be disseminated intravascular coagulation and compartment syndrome. Rhabdomyolysis can also cause metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, hyperphosphatemia, and hyperuricemia. Small vessel obstruction produces the symptoms of fever, pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, and hemoptysis. However, this patient's signs and symptoms are consistent with the diagnosis of liver injury. Option D- Encephalitis: Encephalitis is an inflammatory condition of the tissue of the brain. questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of shortness of breath and fatigue for the past 2 weeks. He was diagnosed with CKD 3 years ago. The laboratory results revealed anemia. Which of the following is the cause of this patient's current condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Decreased erythropoietin: Chronic kidney disease results from the gradual decline in the function of the kidney function. Besides maintaining the electrolyte balance and excretion of metabolic wastes, the kidneys are also involved in the metabolism and management of hormones. Erythropoietin is one of the hormones that plays an essential role in the proliferation and differentiation of red blood cells. In chronic kidney disease, there is a failure of the production of erythropoietin which results in anemia. The anemia can result in the symptoms of shortness of breath, fatigue, and tiredness. On physical examination, the patient will look pale. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hemolysis: Hemolysis can destroy the red blood cells causing anemia which can produce the symptoms of shortness of breath and fatigue. Some of the causes of hemolysis are infections, genetic disease, DIC, etc. However, in chronic kidney disease patients, the anemia is caused by the absence of erythropoietin. Option B- Iron deficiency: Iron deficiency is one of the common causes of anemia which can result in microcytic anemia. Some of the causes of iron deficiency anemia are malabsorption, dietary deficiency, infections, heavy menstrual bleeding, tumors, etc. Option C- Bone marrow fibrosis: Bone marrow fibrosis can also cause anemia because bone marrow is the main site for the production of red blood cells. In this condition, the bone marrow is replaced by connective tissue. Tear-shaped red blood cells can result from bone marrow fibrosis. This patient's anemia is not due to bone marrow fibrosis, instead, it is caused by the absence of erythropoietin. @Neet_pg_bot
