questions.solution: Correct Option D- Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): The eGFR estimates how well the kidneys function and is an important measure of kidney function in potential donors. A low eGFR may indicate underlying renal dysfunction and preclude a donor from donating . Generally, donors with an eGFR of less than 80 mL/min/1.73m2 are not eligible for donation , but the criteria for eGFR may vary depending on the transplant center. Evaluating potential kidney donors involves a comprehensive assessment of the donor's medical history, physical examination, and laboratory tests, including kidney function tests such as serum creatinine, creatinine clearance, and eGFR. Other important considerations in evaluating potential kidney donors may include the donor's age, medical history, family history of renal disease, blood type, and HLA matching with the recipient. Considering this case, eGFR is a critical measure of kidney function that must be evaluated to ensure that the donor has normal kidney function and is not at increased risk of developing kidney disease in the future. questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a history of hypertension and recurrent urinary tract infections. Imaging reveals bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts in each kidney. Which of the following clinical features is a complication of polycystic kidney disease?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a history of hypertension and recurrent urinary tract infections. Imaging reveals bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts in each kidney. Which of the following clinical features is a complication of polycystic kidney disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Hematuria Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is a genetic disorder characterized by developing multiple cysts in the kidneys. The two most common forms of PKD are autosomal dominant PKD (ADPKD) and autosomal recessive PKD (ARPKD). ADPKD is the most common form and is caused by mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes. Hematuria, or blood in the urine, is a common clinical feature of PKD and can occur in up to 50% of patients. It is typically painless and can be microscopic or macroscopic. The cause of hematuria in PKD is thought to be due to the rupture of the cysts, which can cause bleeding into the urine. Incorrect options: Option A: Nephrotic syndrome Nephrotic syndrome, or a group of symptoms including proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia, is not a complication of PKD. Nephrotic syndrome is commonly associated with glomerular diseases such as membranous nephropathy or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Option C: Proteinuria Proteinuria, or excess protein in the urine, is a common finding in patients with PKD, but it is not a complication of the disease. Proteinuria in PKD is usually mild and is not associated with nephrotic syndrome. Option D: Renal cell carcinoma Renal cell carcinoma is a type of kidney cancer that arises from the renal tubular epithelium. While individuals with ADPKD are at increased risk of developing renal cystadenomas (benign tumors arising from the renal tubules), there is no evidence to suggest that they are at increased risk of renal cell carcinoma. @Neet_pg_bot

Immunohistochemical staining shows positive staining for CD10 and negative staining for cytokeratin 7. What is the most likely subtype of renal cell carcinoma?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma Based on the clinical presentation, imaging studies, and immunohistochemical staining pattern, the most likely subtype of renal cell carcinoma is clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC). This subtype of renal cell carcinoma is the most common, accounting for approximately 75% of all cases. It typically presents with necrosis and calcifications on imaging studies and is characterized by the presence of clear cytoplasm due to the accumulation of lipids and glycogen. Positive staining for CD10 is a characteristic feature of clear cell renal cell carcinoma, while negative staining for cytokeratin 7 can help differentiate it from other subtypes of renal cell carcinoma, such as papillary and chromophobe. Clear cell RCC is associated with mutations in the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) gene, which regulates hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) and the oxygen-sensing pathway. Incorrect options: Option B: Papillary renal cell carcinoma Papillary RCC is the second most common type of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for approximately 10-15% of all cases. It typically presents as a mass in the kidney and can be associated with hematuria and flank pain. In imaging studies, it is characterized by cystic areas within the tumor. The tumor cells have a papillary growth pattern and can be classified into two subtypes: type 1 and type 2. Type 1 tumors have a better prognosis than type 2 tumors. Papillary renal cell carcinoma is associated with mutations in the MET proto-oncogene, which is involved in cell proliferation and survival. Option C: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma Chromophobe RCC is a rare subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for approximately 5% of all cases. It typically presents as a mass in the kidney and can be associated with hematuria and flank pain. On imaging studies, it is characterized by a well-circumscribed mass with a homogeneous appearance. The tumor cells have pale, eosinophilic cytoplasm and a perinuclear halo. Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is associated with mutations in the gene encoding for the mitochondrial protein, succinate dehydrogenase (SDHB). Option D: Collecting duct carcinoma Collecting duct carcinoma is a rare subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for less than 1% of all cases. It typically presents as a mass in the kidney and can be associated with hematuria, flank pain, and fever. On imaging studies, it is characterized by a poorly defined mass with irregular borders. The tumors have a glandular or tubular growth pattern and can resemble transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. Collecting duct carcinoma is associated with mutations in genes involved in the maintenance of the collecting ducts of the kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Isoniazid This patient has drug-induced lupus from ingesting isoniazid. She reports having a pre-employment screening and chest X-ray and was presumably found to have a positive tuberculin skin test before starting a prophylactic course of isoniazid. The most common drugs known to cause drug-induced lupus are isoniazid, hydralazine, and procainamide. Numerous other drugs (e.g. penicillamine, methyldopa, quinidine, and sulfasalazine) have also been implicated. questions.solution: Correct Option A - M. Marinum Given this patient’s recent exposure to an aquarium and granulomatous formation, he most likely has “aquarium granuloma” caused by M. marinum. M. marinum causes a localized infection with wound exposure to fresh or salt water (e.g. from swimming pools, fish tanks, water towers) but is under-diagnosed secondary to poor history. It creates characteristic tender red or blue subcutaneous granulomas that extend up the arm, spread along the lymphatics, and may clinically appear like sporotrichosis. Incorrect Options: Option B - M. gordonae: M. gordonae is also found ubiquitously within water systems; it is a major laboratory water contaminant and can create a false positive reporting of acid-fast bacteria in patients with suspected TB. Option C - M. kansasii: M. Kansasii is another important Runyon group I photochromogenic organism and mimics TB in immunocompromised patients. It is the second most common nontuberculous mycobacteria found in HIV patients, surpassed only by M. avium complex. Option D - M. ulcerans: M. ulcerans is another cutaneous mycobacterial lesion that clinically presents as a painless boil which ulcerates and can progress into avascular coagulation necrosis. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Direct viral cytopathic effect on endothelial cells.
questions.solution: Correct Answer: C- Direct viral cytopathic effect on endothelial cells: Dengue Shock Syndrome (DSS) in severe dengue is primarily attributed to a direct viral cytopathic effect on endothelial cells. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypersensitivity reaction leading to capillary leak: Hypersensitivity reactions are not the primary mechanism in DSS. The direct viral effect on endothelial cells is the key factor in plasma leakage. Option B- Activation of the coagulation cascade causing disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC): Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is not the primary mechanism. While coagulation abnormalities can occur in severe dengue, they are secondary to endothelial dysfunction. Option D- Immune complex deposition in small vessels: Immune complex deposition is not a prominent feature of Dengue Shock Syndrome. The pathogenesis is more related to direct viral effects on endothelial cells. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following HIV-resistance mutations increases resistance to the protease inhibitor atazanavir and increases susceptibility to the remaining protease inhibitor antiretroviral drugs?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - I50L Testing for susceptibility as well as resistance to various agents is part of the initial workup for most infectious diseases. When a person is initially diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, an initial round of resistance testing should always be performed in order to ensure the correct antiretroviral agents are selected for the particular patient. There are some common mutations that the clinician should note. The I50L mutation confers strong resistance to the protease inhibitor atazanavir yet simultaneously makes the virus much more sensitive to the remaining drugs in the protease inhibitor class. Incorrect Options: Option A - D30N: Another well-known mutation in protease inhibitors is the D30N mutation, which results in resistance specifically to the protease inhibitor nelfinavir, with no other effects on sensitivities to the other agents in the class. Option C - K65R: The K65R-resistance mutation in HIV increases sensitivity of the virus to zidovudine while simultaneously making it more resistant to tenofovir. The majority of the resistance is toward tenofovir drug combinations such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, tenofovir alafenamide, and (to a lesser extent) abacavir and lamivudine. Option D - K103N: The K103N-resistance mutation is observed in the vast majority of cases in which the virus develops resistance to both efavirenz and nevirapine specifically. However, some of the newer NNRTIs (etravirine and rilpivirine) retain susceptibility to viral strains with K103N. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oral fidaxomicin: Fidaxomicin, a member of the macrolide class of antibiotics, has been associated with a decreased rate of recurrence, in addition to a shorter time until infection resolution in the treatment of hospital-acquired C. difficile. Although some studies portray the recurrence rates of vancomycin and metronidazole as similar, many studies show that the recurrence rates of metronidazole are even higher than vancomycin. Finally, consider using other agents besides vancomycin in order to minimize the alarming emergence of vancomycin-resistant enterococci in the health care setting. questions.solution: Correct Option B- Trophozoite stage: The trophozoite stage of the malarial parasites is responsible for the clinical symptoms of malaria. During this stage, the parasites actively invade and multiply within red blood cells, leading to the characteristic fever, chills, and other systemic manifestations. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Aspirin 75 mg OD: This patient does not satisfy the criteria for antiphospholipid antibodies. questions.stem: Early treatment is necessary for SLE and can be initiated by a physician. Which medication would be an appropriate first choice for SLE arthritis pain?
questions.stemHtml: Early treatment is necessary for SLE and can be initiated by a physician. Which medication would be an appropriate first choice for SLE arthritis pain?

options.label: B
options.text: A combination of hydroxychloroquine plus glucocorticoid

options.label: C
options.text: A combination of glucocorticoid plus immunosuppressant

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Hydroxychloroquine: Antimalarial and low-dose glucocorticoids are first-line agents used to treat arthritis pain associated with SLE. Hydroxychloroquine is the first choice since it reduces disease flares and spares the systemic adverse effects of glucocorticoids. Hydroxychloroquine will reduce constitutional symptoms, musculoskeletal symptoms, and skin manifestations. Incorrect Options: Option A - NSAID (non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs): NSAIDs can be used as an adjunctive therapy but should not be used as monotherapy. NSAIDs are commonly used to manage pain and inflammation associated with arthritis. However, in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), NSAIDs should be used with caution. While they can provide relief from pain and inflammation, they may not be the best initial choice due to the potential for renal involvement and increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, especially in individuals with lupus nephritis or other kidney-related complications. Option B - A combination of hydroxychloroquine plus glucocorticoid: This combination is used for arthritic pain when hydroxychloroquine monotherapy has failed. Hydroxychloroquine is indeed a medication commonly used to treat SLE due to its immunomodulatory effects. However, in the context of arthritis pain management, it might not be the first-line choice because its onset of action can be slower, and its primary role in SLE management is to control overall disease activity rather than provide rapid pain relief. Glucocorticoids (steroids) can provide rapid relief from inflammation and pain, but they are often used cautiously due to potential side effects with long-term use, including bone loss and increased infection risk. Option C - A combination of glucocorticoid plus immunosuppressant: This combination is used for SLE patients with renal manifestations. While glucocorticoids can provide fast relief from inflammation and pain, they are typically used in SLE as part of a broader treatment plan and often at the lowest effective dose due to their potential side effects. questions.stem: An 87-year-old woman comes for a routine clinic appointment. She has mild rheumatoid arthritis well controlled on DMARD therapy. Recently, while on holiday, she fell and was bruised across her cheeks and nose. Several weeks later, this apparent bruising has not recovered, and she still has gray discoloration across her face. Which medication is she likely to be taking?

Recently, while on holiday, she fell and was bruised across her cheeks and nose. Several weeks later, this apparent bruising has not recovered, and she still has gray discoloration across her face. Which medication is she likely to be taking?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Minocycline: Minocycline is tetracycline used predominantly in the treatment of acne and rosacea. However several studies have shown an improvement in joint tenderness and swelling in patients with rheumatoid arthritis taking minocycline 200 mg od compared to placebo. Therefore, while it is not commonly used in rheumatology, there is a cohort of RA patients who remain on it. It is well known to cause pigmentation primarily affecting the skin but also reported in other tissues (bones, cartilage, thyroid, heart valves, substantia nigra, atherosclerotic plaques etc), There are four reported site-specific types and combinations of these types have also been reported. Type I does not appear to be dose or duration-dependent and pigmentation has been reported with as little as 8 g, however, it is most common with cumulative doses >100 g. Tissue damage appears to predispose, so trauma, sun exposure, age, and steroid use all increase the risk of pigmentation. Type I will generally fade over months or years on cessation of minocycline, but this is less likely with types II and III. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Rapid, multiplex, real-time PCR Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2 and L3, which are distinct from those that cause the more common form of Chlamydial disease (serovars D-K). The LGV strains are most often found in Africa, Southeastern Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Sporadic cases of LGV have occurred in North America, although these are thought to have been imported. During the first phase of the infection, patients present with an ulcerative disease. These ulcers are usually small and of short duration. After the resolution of the ulcers, there are two main presentations of this disease: the classical inguinal syndrome as well as the anorectal syndrome. In the inguinal syndrome, the bacteria spread via the lymphatic system to cause inguinal lymphadenopathy with the formation of buboes. If the disease is left untreated, the surrounding tissue structures can be destroyed, leading to fistulas and damage to the lymphatic system. In severe cases, it may result in elephantiasis. Typical anorectal symptoms include spasms, perianal sores, bloody discharge, pain, and constipation (as in this case). Multiplex real-time PCR is specific for the detection of LGV associated L-serovars and enables the differentiation of L1, L2, and L3 for epidemiologic studies. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Homogentisic Acid Accumulation: The underlying mechanism of the patient's disease is homogentisic acid accumulation, which leads to a condition known as alkaptonuria. Alkaptonuria is a rare metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase. This enzyme is required for the breakdown of tyrosine, and its deficiency leads to the accumulation of homogentisic acid in the body. This acid is then excreted in the urine, giving it a dark color. Ochronosis is a key feature of alkaptonuria, leading to the deposition of homogentisic acid-derived pigments in connective tissues, including cartilage, tendons, and the sclera of the eyes. questions.answerText: Activation of central and peripheral melanocortin receptors
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Activation of central and peripheral melanocortin receptors: More recently, it has been shown that ACTH activates central and peripheral melanocortin receptors. Incorrect Options: Option A - Modulation of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor: Fingolimod is approved as a disease-modifying drug for MS. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Wake up and go outside as soon as it is morning in France: Treatment of jet lag involves measures to help adjust one’s circadian rhythm to the new time zone. Adjusting to the French time zone involves advancing the circadian rhythm (i.e. going to sleep earlier than one normally would in the United States). Bright light in the morning is a strong stimulus to advance the circadian rhythm. Keeping a regular wake-up time in the morning and going outside, starting the day on the usual French schedule would be the best way to adjust to the new time zone as quickly as possible. Incorrect Options: Option A - A glass of wine with dinner each night: Although alcohol shortens sleep latency it leads to problems with sleep maintenance and overall worsens quality of sleep. Option B - Going to sleep whenever they feel tired and wake up when they are rested: Going to bed when they feel tired and sleeping until they are rested will delay entrainment to the new schedule. Option D - Take melatonin as soon as it is morning in France: Melatonin at night can help advance the sleep phase. Melatonin in the morning may actually delay the circadian clock further in addition to having sedative effects which could make them more tired during the day. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Direct drainage into a cortical vein: Dural arteriovenous fistulas are pathologic vascular shunts that connect dural arteries to the intracranial venous system. Option C - Direct drainage into the dural venous sinus: Dural AV fistulas are abnormal connections between arteries and veins in the dura mater (the outermost layer of the brain covering). Option D - Origin from the middle meningeal artery: The origin from the middle meningeal artery is mentioned in the clinical scenario, as the dural AV fistula is fed from the right middle meningeal artery. However, this feature is not specifically associated with the risk of hemorrhage. Option E - Retrograde flow into subarachnoid veins: Retrograde flow refers to blood flow in the opposite direction, from veins to arteries. questions.stem: Beyond genetic testing, which of the following diagnostic tests is often used when considering a diagnosis of Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)?
questions.stemHtml: Beyond genetic testing, which of the following diagnostic tests is often used when considering a diagnosis of Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Skin biopsy: The diagnosis of CADASIL is made with the combination of clinical history, exam, MRI findings, skin biopsy and genetic testing. Although sequencing of the NOTCH3 gene is the gold standard diagnostic test, skin biopsy may also help make the diagnosis due to the involvement of systemic arterioles in addition to the central nervous system vasculature. Electron microscopy of the skin biopsy may show granular osmiophilic material near the basement membrane of arteriole smooth muscle cells. The use of NOTCH3 antibodies may increase the sensitivity of skin biopsy. The other choices have not been systematically assessed for diagnosis of CADASIL and are more invasive and higher risk than skin biopsy. Nonetheless, these changes are present in nerve and muscle tissue as well (see link below) and one could consider evaluating arterioles in these tissues in an individual suspected to have the illness if the tissue is already available for an alternative purpose. Incorrect Options: Option A - Liver biopsy: Liver biopsy is not used for the diagnosis of CADASIL. CADASIL primarily affects the brain and small blood vessels, and liver biopsy is not relevant to this condition. Option C - Muscle biopsy: Muscle biopsy is not a standard diagnostic test for CADASIL. The condition primarily involves the brain's small blood vessels, and muscle biopsy would not provide relevant information for this diagnosis. Option D - Nerve biopsy: Nerve biopsy is not routinely used for the diagnosis of CADASIL. The disease primarily affects the cerebral arteries and small blood vessels in the brain, and nerve biopsy is not a standard procedure for evaluating this condition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: You are asked to consult on a newborn in the intensive care unit who is microcephalic and hypotonic. Imaging studies reveal intracranial calcifications, but urine testing for CMV DNA by PCR is negative. Which of the following is most likely to be the cause of this child’s neurological manifestations?
questions.stemHtml: You are asked to consult on a newborn in the intensive care unit who is microcephalic and hypotonic. Imaging studies reveal intracranial calcifications, but urine testing for CMV DNA by PCR is negative. Which of the following is most likely to be the cause of this child’s neurological manifestations?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Congenital toxoplasmosis: Intracranial calcifications are most commonly seen in congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) and congenital toxoplasmosis infections, and more recently have been noted as a characteristic finding in Zika virus infection. Calcifications tend to be periventricular in CMV, diffuse in toxoplasmosis, and subcortical in Zika virus infection. The other infections may have neurological sequelae, such as encephalitis or autistic disorders and rarely calcifications in congenital rubella, and meningitis and cranial neuropathies in syphilis, while congenital HIV infection does not usually cause neurological deficits that are appreciable at birth. Incorrect Options: Option A - Congenital Rubeola Infection: Congenital rubella infection can lead to various neurological manifestations in newborns, but intracranial calcifications are not typically a prominent feature. Instead, congenital rubella infection can cause sensorineural deafness, congenital heart defects, cataracts, and other systemic abnormalities. Option B - Congenital HIV Infection: Congenital HIV infection can lead to neurodevelopmental abnormalities in newborns. However, the presence of intracranial calcifications is not a typical feature of congenital HIV infection. Neurological manifestations in congenital HIV infection can include developmental delays, seizures, and encephalopathy. Option D - Aicardi-Goutières Syndrome: Aicardi-Goutières syndrome is a rare genetic disorder that can cause progressive neurological symptoms and brain calcifications. However, it typically presents with more generalized encephalopathy, abnormal white matter on brain imaging, and other clinical features beyond microcephaly and hypotonia. Aicardi-Goutieres Syndrome is a group of genetic disorders that mimic TORCH infections, often with intracranial calcifications, but typically present after the perinatal period and may have a progressive or relapsing/progressive course. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following regarding the disease-modifying medication ocrelizumab is false?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following regarding the disease-modifying medication ocrelizumab is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately 25% of patients experience infusion-related reactions

options.label: B
options.text: It decreases relapse rates in relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis

options.label: C
options.text: It has been shown to reactivate latent hepatitis B

options.label: D
options.text: It improves walking speed in primary progressive multiple sclerosis

questions.answerText: It improves walking speed in primary progressive multiple sclerosis
questions.solution: Correct Option D - It improves walking speed in primary progressive multiple sclerosis: Ocrelizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 receptor on B-cells and results in cellular lysis. It is approved for both relapsing remitting and primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS). In clinical trials, ocrelizumab slows disability progression in patients with PPMS. However, patients did not have improvement in their clinical disability. Incorrect Options: Option A - Approximately 25% of Patients Experience Infusion-Related Reactions: This statement is true. Infusion-related reactions are common with ocrelizumab, particularly during the first infusion. These reactions can include symptoms such as itching, rash, fever, chills, and headache. Most of these reactions are mild to moderate in severity and can be managed with premedications and adjusting the infusion rate. Option B - It Decreases Relapse Rates in Relapsing Remitting Multiple Sclerosis: This statement is true. Ocrelizumab is a disease-modifying therapy approved for the treatment of relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (MS), including relapsing-remitting MS. It has been shown to significantly reduce relapse rates, delay disability progression, and slow the accumulation of disability in patients with relapsing forms of MS. Option C - It has been shown to reactivate latent hepatitis B: Ocrelizumab is associated with reactivation of latent hepatitis B. Therefore, all patients should be tested for hepatitis B prior to treatment. Mild infusion reactions (headache, fatigue, nausea) are common and improve with subsequent infusions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis presents for evaluation of 2 days of right leg weakness. Her exam shows normal vital signs, mild right leg spasticity, moderate right ankle dorsiflexor weakness, and decreased vibration in the right foot. She denies recent fever of chills, upper respiratory symptoms or dysuria but admits to increased urinary frequency in the past 3 days. What is the next best step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis presents for evaluation of 2 days of right leg weakness. Her exam shows normal vital signs, mild right leg spasticity, moderate right ankle dorsiflexor weakness, and decreased vibration in the right foot. She denies recent fever of chills, upper respiratory symptoms or dysuria but admits to increased urinary frequency in the past 3 days. What is the next best step in management?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Check a urinalysis: The majority of patients with multiple sclerosis have the relapsing-remitting form of the disease. Relapses are usually defined as new or worsening neurological symptoms and/or signs that last more than 24 hours in the absence of fever or infection. The presence of new or worsening symptoms in the setting of an infection is termed as pseudo exacerbation. This patient denies dysuria but has noted increased urinary frequency which can be a symptom of a urinary tract infection (UTI). In addition, patients with MS often have a history of spinal cord pathology which may cause them not to present with typical UTI symptoms. In this case, evaluation for possible UTI as a cause for pseudo exacerbation is the best next step in management. Incorrect Options: Option A- Start IV methylprednisolone Methylprednisolone and prednisone are sometimes used in the treatment MS relapses, however, differentiating between a true relapse and a pseudo exacerbation is the best next step in management before initiating any therapy. Option C- Start oral prednisone: Similar to IV methylprednisolone, oral prednisone is used to manage acute exacerbations of multiple sclerosis. However, it's important to establish the underlying cause of the new symptoms before deciding on specific treatment. Option D- Referral for rehabilitation: Referral for rehabilitation is not an appropriate next step at this stage. After the patient has been evaluated and treated a referral to rehabilitation may be indicated depending on the degree of residual symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 42-year-old male comes to the clinic complaining of abdominal pain. He reports a 5-month history of epigastric pain that improves with meals. He has lost 15 pounds since the pain started. His past medical history is significant for a prolactinoma for which he underwent transsphenoidal resection. He drinks alcohol socially and has a 10-pack-year smoking history. His family history is notable for a maternal uncle with a parathyroid adenoma. His vitals are within the normal range. After further workup, the patient is started on octreotide, an analogue of an endogenously produced hormone. When this hormone is produced by the hypothalamus, it has which of the following effects?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old male comes to the clinic complaining of abdominal pain. He reports a 5-month history of epigastric pain that improves with meals. He has lost 15 pounds since the pain started. His past medical history is significant for a prolactinoma for which he underwent transsphenoidal resection. He drinks alcohol socially and has a 10-pack-year smoking history. His family history is notable for a maternal uncle with a parathyroid adenoma. His vitals are within the normal range. After further workup, the patient is started on octreotide, an analogue of an endogenously produced hormone. When this hormone is produced by the hypothalamus, it has which of the following effects?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Decrease the production of growth hormone: Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, is used to treat various neuroendocrine tumours, such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (as seen in this patient) and carcinoid tumours. When somatostatin is produced by the hypothalamus, it functions to inhibit the production and release of growth hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Somatostatin is produced by multiple tissues and has variable inhibitory effects depending on the tissue upon which it is acting. When it is produced in the gastrointestinal tract, somatostatin functions to decrease gastric secretion and gallbladder contraction. When it is produced in the endocrine pancreas, somatostatin functions to decrease insulin and glucagon release. When it is produced in the hypothalamus, it inhibits the production and release of growth hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Incorrect Options: Option A - Decrease production of cholecystokinin: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a GI hormone that is produced in the duodenum in response to fatty acids and amino acids. CCK increases pancreatic secretion, gallbladder contraction, and gastric emptying. Somatostatin from the gastrointestinal tract, not the hypothalamus, inhibits CCK release by inhibiting the secretion of CCK-releasing peptides. Option C - Decrease the production of prolactin: Prolactin is released from the anterior pituitary and functions to stimulate milk production and inhibits ovulation or spermatogenesis. Its release is inhibited by dopamine from the hypothalamus. Option D - Decrease the production of gastrin: Gastrin is secreted by G cells in the stomach antrum and increases gastric H+ secretion and gastric motility. Somatostatin from the gastrointestinal tract, not the hypothalamus, will decrease gastrin secretion. @Neet_pg_bot

Laboratory tests reveal an elevated serum prolactin level. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Bromocriptine: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist that can reduce prolactin secretion and shrink pituitary adenomas by increasing tonic dopamine signalling to inhibit lactotrophs in the anterior pituitary. This patient presents with symptoms consistent with hyperprolactinemia, including headaches, irregular periods, and decreased libido. An elevated serum prolactin level is confirmed by laboratory tests. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient would be bromocriptine. Incorrect Options: Option A - Estrogen: ERT is primarily used to treat symptoms associated with menopause, such as hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and osteoporosis. Estrogen replacement therapy (ERT) would not be appropriate for a patient with a prolactinoma or hyperprolactinemia, as in this patient, because it can stimulate the growth of pituitary tumours and increase prolactin secretion. Option C - Methyldopa: Methyldopa is not an appropriate treatment for a patient with a prolactinoma or hyperprolactinemia, as it can further increase prolactin levels by suppressing dopamine production. questions.stem: A 21-year-old female presented with truncal obesity with a moon face and buffalo hump. On examination, purple striae and muscle wasting are present. An endocrinologist wants to investigate by determining the blood levels of hormones and electrolytes. What is suspected in this case of Cushing syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old female presented with truncal obesity with a moon face and buffalo hump. On examination, purple striae and muscle wasting are present. An endocrinologist wants to investigate by determining the blood levels of hormones and electrolytes. What is suspected in this case of Cushing syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - High cortisol and low ACTH: Cushing syndrome involves the excess of all adrenal hormones. It is diagnosed by: Demonstration of high cortisol level Serum ACTH levels Dexamethasone suppression test Salivary cortisol 24-hour urinary-free cortisol Radiologic imaging. The outpatient initial screening test is 24-hour urinary-free cortisol. The best initial diagnostic test is an overnight dexamethasone suppression test followed by a 1 mg loading dose. To localise the lesion, a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is carried out to differentiate between pituitary adenoma and ectopic source. If ACTH is low and cortisol is high, there is either an adrenal adenoma or exogenous glucocorticoid intake. However, if ACTH is high and cortisol is low, then there is either pituitary adenoma or an ectopic source that secretes ACTH, such as small cell cancer of the lung. If the cortisol levels are suppressed, followed by a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, the cause is a pituitary adenoma. Contrarily, if no suppression has occurred, the cause is an ectopic source of ACTH. Incorrect Options: Option B - High cortisol and high ACTH: If ACTH is high and cortisol is also high, there is either pituitary adenoma (Cushing’s disease) or an ectopic source that secretes ACTH, such as small cell cancer of the lung. Option C - Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia: In Cushing syndrome, there is an excess aldosterone secretion that results in hypernatremia and hypokalemia. Option D - Decreased urinary free cortisol: Increased urinary-free cortisol is present in Cushing syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 24-year-old female presented with muscle wasting, glucose intolerance, and hypertension. On examination, purplish striae, moon-like face, and buffalo hump are noticed. After investigation, the cause of Cushing syndrome has been adrenal adenoma. What is the treatment of choice in such a case?
questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old female presented with muscle wasting, glucose intolerance, and hypertension. On examination, purplish striae, moon-like face, and buffalo hump are noticed. After investigation, the cause of Cushing syndrome has been adrenal adenoma. What is the treatment of choice in such a case?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Adrenalectomy: In the above scenario, Cushing syndrome is caused by adrenal adenoma. This is characterised by a high level of adrenal hormones, i.e. excessive synthesis of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and androgens. Removal of the cause of hypercortisolism is the main treatment. In the case of primary adrenal hyperfunction due to a tumour, surgical removal is indicated. Management of adrenalectomy patients requires adequate preoperative and postoperative replacement therapy with corticosteroids. Tumours that produce corticosteroids usually lead to atrophy of the normal adrenal; therefore, replacement with cortisol is required until there is a recovery of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Postoperative complications may include sepsis, thrombosis, sudden collapse, and poor wound healing. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cyproheptadine: In pituitary cushing disease, cyproheptadine and bromocriptine effectively lower ACTH levels. Cyproheptadine is a centrally acting serotonin receptor antagonist that blocks ACTH release in Cushing disease. Option C - Paseriotide: It is a somatostatin analogue given in adults with persistent disease after surgery or in whom surgery is contraindicated. Option D - Irradiation: Irradiation is carried out in patients with Pituitary microadenomas. @Neet_pg_bot

His serum aldosterone level is found to be elevated. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Primary aldosteronism: The clinical scenario described in the question is consistent with the features of hyperaldosteronism, a disorder that results in excess production of aldosterone from the adrenal gland. The most likely cause of hyperaldosteronism in this patient is primary aldosteronism, which is also known as Conn's syndrome. This condition results in increased aldosterone production, leading to hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. It is the most common cause of secondary hypertension, accounting for approximately 10% of all cases. Patients with primary aldosteronism may present with symptoms such as fatigue, muscle weakness, and polyuria. Diagnosis is made through measurement of aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR), which is typically elevated in primary aldosteronism. Treatment includes aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone or eplerenone. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cushing's syndrome: Cushing's syndrome is an adrenal disorder characterized by excess cortisol production. While it can lead to hypertension and electrolyte disturbances, it is not associated with hyperaldosteronism. Option C - Addison's disease: Addison's disease is caused by adrenal insufficiency and results in decreased cortisol and aldosterone production. It typically presents with fatigue, weight loss, and hypotension, and is not associated with hyperaldosteronism. Option D - Hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism is not typically associated with hyperaldosteronism. While thyroid hormone levels can affect renal function and blood pressure, the symptoms described in the scenario are not consistent with hypothyroidism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of difficulty driving at night and bilateral blurry vision which is progressive for five months. A slit lamp reveals bilateral cloudy opacities of the lens. Increased activity of which of the following enzyme is the cause of the patient's current pathology?
questions.solution: Option B - Aldose reductase: This is a case of poorly-controlled diabetes mellitus in which the patient presents with complaints of difficulty driving at night and bilateral blurry vision which is progressive for five months. The patient is a known case of hyperlipidemia, type-2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. The Haemoglobin A 1C concentration of the patient is 8.8%. A slit lamp test of the patient was done which reveals bilateral cloudy opacities of the lens which is most likely due to poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. The increased activity of aldose reductase is the cause of the patient's pathology. The reduction of glucose to sorbitol is catalysed by the aldose reductase enzyme , then sorbitol is oxidised to fructose by an enzyme called sorbitol dehydrogenase . Only a little amount of glucose is metabolised by this polyol pathway when the blood glucose level is normal. In chronic hyperglycemia , there is increased sorbitol formation which results in osmotic damage in tissues of the retina, lens, kidney and myelin sheaths . Consequently, the patient may present with nephropathy, peripheral neuropathy, retinopathy and bilateral cataracts . Correct Options: Option A - Aldolase B: Aldolase B is usually expressed in the liver . It helps in the conversion of fructose-1-phosphate to glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. The deficiency of this enzyme results in hereditary fructose intolerance which usually presents with vomiting and hypoglycemia. Option C - Sorbitol dehydrogenase: Sorbitol dehydrogenase is an enzyme which helps in the conversion of sorbitol into fructose. It is used as an energy substrate in seminal vesicles and the liver . Increased activity of sorbitol dehydrogenase is not associated with any specific disease. Option D - Glucokinase: Glucokinase is an isoenzyme which is predominantly present in beta cells of the pancreas and liver. It helps in insulin secretion and promotes glucose storage , respectively. It is not associated with cataract formation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A patient complains of loss of appetite, early satiety, flatulence, and bloating one year after ileocecectomy for Crohn’s disease. Physical exam and laboratory studies, including fecal tests, are within normal limits except for hemoglobin 10 mg/dL and macrocytosis. Colonoscopy is normal. You suspect small bowel intestinal overgrowth. Which of the following is the next step to determine if this is the correct diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Lactulose breath test: A diagnosis of small intestine bowel overgrowth can be made in patients for whom there is clinical suspicion by a positive culture of jejunal aspirate or by a positive breath test. Carbohydrate breath tests most commonly use glucose or lactulose as a substrate. A lactulose breath test is considered positive if there is an absolute increase in hydrogen of 20 ppm or more above the baseline within 90 minutes, methane of 3 ppm or greater at any time during the test, or a double peak pattern of an early increase in production of hydrogen with a later colonic peak after 2 hours. Incorrect Options: Option A - Gastric biopsy : Jejunal biopsy, not gastric, is used to diagnose SIBO. A bacterial concentration of >10^3 colony-forming units/mL of jejunal aspirate is diagnostic of SIBO. Option B - Video capsule enteroscopy : Enteroscopy is not necessary to make the diagnosis of SIBO but may be used to exclude other possible pathology. Option C - IgA endomysial antibody : In patients with a negative hydrogen test, celiac disease should be considered in the differential. Symptoms are similar, and patients with both disorders may have elevated fecal fat with villous blunting on biopsy of the small bowel. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient with dysphagia undergoes high-resolution manometry. Esophageal pressure topography reveals a type I OGJ, integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) of 10 mmHg, and distal latency of 5.8 seconds. His study indicates distal contractile integral (DCI) of 9000 mm/s/cm on 2 swallows with single-peaked contraction. This is characteristic of which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A patient with dysphagia undergoes high-resolution manometry. Esophageal pressure topography reveals a type I OGJ, integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) of 10 mmHg, and distal latency of 5.8 seconds. His study indicates distal contractile integral (DCI) of 9000 mm/s/cm on 2 swallows with single-peaked contraction. This is characteristic of which of the following?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Jackhammer esophagus: Jackhammer or hypercontractile esophagus is characterized by 2/10 test swallows with a DCI >8000 mm/s/cm. The Chicago Classification scheme of esophageal motility diagnosis categorizes motility disorders based on esophageal pressure topography studies. EGJ morphology is not a defining criteria for motility studies but can identify a hiatus hernia. A hiatus hernia can distort EPT metrics. Basal EGJ pressure is also not a defining criterion but in some disorders it can be pertinent, including GERD and achalasia. Type I EGJ is normal. IRP is based on the median value of 10 test swallows and is a major diagnostic criterion for achalasia and EGJ outflow obstruction. Integrated relaxation pressure measures adequacy of LES relaxation with swallowing. Abnormal IRP is consistent with esophageal motility disorders and is defined as the average minimum EGJ pressure for 4 seconds within seconds of swallowing. In patients with hypercontractile esophagus, the IRP is normal. The upper limit of normal is 15 mmHg. Incorrect Options: Option A - Normal esophageal motility: The DCI is elevated in >20% of test swallows, indicating hypercontractile jackhammer esophagus. Option B - GERD: GERD is not a motility disorder of the esophagus. Option D - Type I achalasia: Patients with type I achalasia have an IRP at or above the upper limit of normal, and no contractility is present. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements regarding adenomatous polyps of the stomach is incorrect?

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.answerText: There is no indication for surveillance in patients with adenomatous gastric polyps
questions.solution: Correct Option B - There is no indication for surveillance in patients with adenomatous gastric polyps: Adenomatous polyps of the stomach are associated with an increased risk of developing gastric cancer. Incorrect Options: Option A - They are typically solitary: Adenomatous polyps of the stomach are usually solitary, meaning they occur as a single polyp rather than multiple polyps. Option C - They are associated with an increased incidence of synchronous adenocarcinoma of the stomach: Adenomatous polyps of the stomach are considered premalignant lesions, and they are associated with a higher risk of synchronous adenocarcinoma, which means that the cancer can occur simultaneously with the polyps in the same patient. Option D - They can have varying appearances on endoscopy: Adenomatous polyps of the stomach can have different appearances on endoscopy, including features such as size, shape, and surface characteristics. Some may be flat or sessile, while others may be raised or pedunculated. The endoscopic appearance helps in determining their potential for malignancy and guides the need for further investigation or surveillance. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: C
options.text: Testing for p53 mutations will further clarify this patient’s risk for gastric cancer.

questions.solution: Correct Option D - This patient merits gastric mapping: Gastric mapping refers to a technique where multiple biopsies are taken from different areas of the stomach to identify any abnormalities or early signs of cancer. Incorrect Options: Option A - There is an increased risk for dysplasia within his polyps: Hyperplastic polyps are generally considered to have a very low risk of progressing to dysplasia or cancer. questions.stem: While covering hospital GI consults, you are called to see a patient for evaluation of possible stress ulcer bleeding. Which of the following is true concerning stress ulcer bleeding?
questions.stemHtml: While covering hospital GI consults, you are called to see a patient for evaluation of possible stress ulcer bleeding. Which of the following is true concerning stress ulcer bleeding?

options.label: A
options.text: Pharmacologic prophylaxis is effective for patients receiving enteral nutrition.

options.label: B
options.text: Stress ulceration usually occurs in the antrum or duodenum.

options.label: C
options.text: The primary mechanism of stress ulceration is excessive stimulation of parietal cells by gastrin stimulation.

options.label: D
options.text: Prolonged mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy are the most important risk factors for stress ulcer bleeding.

questions.answerText: Prolonged mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy are the most important risk factors for stress ulcer bleeding.
questions.solution: Option D - Prolonged mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy are the most important risk factors for stress ulcer bleeding: The most important risk factors for stress ulcer bleeding include coagulopathy (defined as a platelet count <50,000/m 3 ) and mechanical ventilation for longer than 48 hours. A history of GI ulcer or GI bleed within the past year, traumatic brain or spinal cord injury, and burn injury are high-risk characteristics that are indications for pharmacologic prophylaxis. Minor criteria include ICU stay >1 week, sepsis, occult GI bleed >6 days, and glucocorticoid therapy greater than the equivalent of 250 mg hydrocortisone. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pharmacologic prophylaxis is effective for patients receiving enteral nutrition: Enteral nutrition may reduce the risk of overt GI bleeding in patients with stress ulcers, but pharmacological prophylaxis may be harmful or ineffective in patients on enteral nutrition. Option B - Stress ulceration usually occurs in the antrum or duodenum: Stress ulcerations initially occur in the proximal portion of the stomach. After several days of hospitalization, stress ulcerations are generally more distal and deeper. Option C - The primary mechanism of stress ulceration is excessive stimulation of parietal cells by gastrin stimulation: Hypersecretion of acid due to excessive parietal cell stimulation by gastrin has been identified in head trauma patients, but this is most likely not the cause of stress ulceration in all ICU patients. Impaired mucosal protection results in critical patients as a result of destruction of the mucosal barrier by increased concentrations of bile salts or uremic toxins. Bicarbonate production that contributes to the mucosal defense barrier may also be diminished due to poor perfusion resulting from trauma, sepsis, or shock. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: The parietal cells secrete pure hydrochloric acid at a concentration equivalent to a pH of 0.8.
questions.solution: Correct Option B - The parietal cells secrete pure hydrochloric acid at a concentration equivalent to a pH of 0.8: Gastric juice is made up of both parietal and non parietal secretions, with parietal cell secretion of pure hydrochloric acid at a concentration equivalent to pH of 0.8. Non Parietal secretions include mucus, electrolytes, and water. Incorrect Options: Option A - Gastric acid is secreted primarily by parietal cells as well as by G cells: G cells release gastrin, which acts on the cholecystokinin receptor of the parietal cell. Option C - Parietal cells have membrane receptors for 4 stimulants: Parietal cells have basolateral membrane receptors for histamine (H2-receptor), acetylcholine (muscarinic M3 cholinergic receptor), and cholecystokinin (CCKB). These are the only receptors for stimulation. Option D - The only inhibitory receptors on the parietal cell are somatostatin receptors: Parietal cells have receptors on the basolateral membrane for inhibitors, including somatostatin and prostaglandins. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Mallory’s hyaline and megamitochondria are findings consistent with which stage of alcoholic liver disease?
questions.stemHtml: Mallory’s hyaline and megamitochondria are findings consistent with which stage of alcoholic liver disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - A and B only: Both Mallory’s hyaline and megamitochondria are seen in alcoholic liver disease. There are changes seen with both alcoholic hepatitis as well as cirrhosis. Mallory’s hyaline is seen in approximately 60% of patients with alcoholic liver disease, while approximately 50% with alcoholic cirrhosis have this finding on liver biopsy. Megamitochondria is seen in 20% of patients with alcoholic hepatitis, while 33% of patients with cirrhosis have it. While it may seem to be associated with more severe alcoholic liver disease, it is actually associated with less severe clinical phenotypes and better clinical outcomes. Both Mallory’s hyaline and megamitochondria are rarely seen in alcoholic fatty liver. Other changes seen under microscopy with cirrhosis include perivenular and perisinusoidal fibrosis . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 48-year-old G5P5 postmenopausal female presents with a complaint of fecal incontinence. Which of the following is true?
questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old G5P5 postmenopausal female presents with a complaint of fecal incontinence. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: About 6% of women over 40 have fecal incontinence

options.label: B
options.text: Sedentary lifestyle is a risk factor for fecal incontinence in young women

options.label: C
options.text: In patients who fail to respond to conservativemeasures, defecography is the next step in management

options.label: D
options.text: Passive incontinence is associated with dysfunction of the internal anal sphincter

questions.answerText: Passive incontinence is associated with dysfunction of the internal anal sphincter
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Passive incontinence is associated with dysfunction of the internal anal sphincter: Fecal incontinence is an involuntary passage of liquid or stool that results in social or hygiene problems. The prevalence in the community is 2-3% and increases with age to over 10%. Fecal incontinence among nursing home patients is estimated at nearly 50%, with a greater prevalence among women. Both anatomic and functional factors contribute to normal continence. Distension of the rectum causes a reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter (IAS) and decreased anal resting pressure. The anal contractile response is the subconscious reflex that prevents release of rectal contents through the external anal sphincter. The primary nerve to the anorectum is the pudendal nerve, which arises from S2, S3, and S4. Sensory, motor, autonomic, and enteric nerves supply the anorectum. Disruption to any of these components may result in fecal incontinence. Passive incontinence is suggestive of dysfunction of the sensory system or the internal anal sphincter. Incorrect Options: Option A - About 6% of women over 40 have fecal incontinence: The prevalence of fecal incontinence in individuals who live in the community is 2-3%. In women less than 40 years of age, the rate of fecal incontinence is 6% and increases to 15% among women over the age of 40. Option B - Sedentary lifestyle is a risk factor for fecal incontinence in young women: High-level sports activity is an independent risk factor in healthy young women. Option C - In patients who fail to respond to conservative measures, defecography is the next step in management: In patients who fail to respond to conservative measures, the potential next steps in evaluation include anorectal manometry with endorectal ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging. Defecography is generally reserved for patients who have refractory symptoms, especially if surgery is being considered. @Neet_pg_bot
